en.blog.antiguedad-de-saldos-lo-que-no-dice: Ageing reports: what that report isn't telling you
Collections
The most-used receivables report is also the most misleading. Three things it hides that decide whether you get paid.
The report everyone looks at
An ageing report splits what you're owed into buckets: current, 30, 60, 90, over 90. It's the most used collections report in the world and, read properly, it's useful.
The trouble is it gets read as if it said who's going to pay you, and it doesn't say that. It says how long each invoice has gone unpaid, which isn't the same thing.
The three things it hides

A customer who's up to date with a big problem. If they pay religiously every month but their total balance has grown 40% in a quarter, the ageing report flags nothing: it's all «current». Your exposure grew and the report doesn't say so.

The difference between not paying and being in dispute. An invoice in the 90-day bucket can be a customer who won't pay or an invoice the customer rejects over a delivery problem. They're handled in completely different ways, and the report puts them together.

The agreed terms. If you gave a customer 60 days, their 45-day invoice isn't overdue even if it lands in an alarming bucket. An ageing report calculated on the invoice date instead of the due date scares you for nothing — and worse: it reassures you when it shouldn't.
Ageing is calculated from the DUE DATE, not from issue. It's the commonest mistake, and it produces a report that looks right and is wrong for every customer on anything other than cash terms.
What else to look at
The trend of each customer's balance, not just the balance. Growth is the early signal; falling overdue is the late one.
The real average collection days against the agreed ones. If you agreed 30 and collect at 52, you're financing the customer for 22 days nobody decided on.
How much of your balance sits with a few customers. A report that's healthy overall can hide that 60% is owed by a single one.
Which invoices are in dispute, flagged as such, with the reason. Chasing by phone an invoice the customer rejected three weeks ago wastes everyone's time twice.
What really decides whether you get paid happened earlier

The uncomfortable conclusion: by the time an invoice shows up in the 90-day bucket, the decisions that mattered have already been made. Who you gave credit to, how much, on what terms, and whether you checked anything first.
That's managed with the credit limit, which is where the problem gets stopped. The ageing report is the thermometer; the limit is the treatment.
Collect earlier, don't chase later
Zyntello Accounts Receivable calculates ageing from the real due date, flags disputed invoices and warns before they fall due.
en.blog.limite-de-credito-que-hace-y-que-no: The credit limit: what it does, what it doesn't, and why it's nearly always bypassed
Customer credit
A limit you can bypass without leaving a trace isn't a limit. How to set one that works without blocking legitimate sales.
What it's really for
A credit limit isn't there to say no. It's there to force someone to decide when a figure is exceeded, instead of letting exposure grow without anyone noticing.
That's the difference between a useful limit and a decorative one: the useful one interrupts. If the system warns but lets you carry on, and nobody reviews those warnings, the limit doesn't exist.
How it gets bypassed in practice
From what we've seen implementing this, the ways around it are always the same:
You invoice some other way. A manual invoice, another point of sale, another company in the group.
The limit gets raised «temporarily» and nobody lowers it. Six months on, the limit is a history of overruns.

The limit doesn't count pending orders. The customer is at 90% of the limit and has three orders still to deliver that will push them over. The system lets them through because they aren't invoices yet.
It's compared against today's balance, not the overdue one. A customer can be within the limit and have everything overdue: the number says yes and reality says no.

The check that reveals whether your limit works: find out how many sales were approved over the limit last quarter, and who approved them. If you can't answer, you don't have a limit: you have a field.
How to set it so it doesn't block sales
The risk on the other side is real: a control that's too rigid turns every sale into paperwork and ends up switched off. What works:
Make approval fast and on the record. One manager, from a phone, in a minute — with a trail of who approved what.
Make the block distinguish reasons. Going over the limit isn't the same as having overdue invoices. The second is more serious and should stop things sooner.
Make it count the total commitment: invoiced plus orders still to deliver.
Review the limit with data. A customer who's paid on time for two years deserves a higher limit; one who's started stretching, a lower one.

And one implementation detail that matters more than it looks: the limit has to live in a single field. We've seen systems with two credit-limit fields inherited from different eras, where one was displayed and the other was validated. The result is a control that looks active and isn't.
A limit that actually stops things
In Zyntello the limit counts invoiced and ordered, distinguishes over-limit from overdue, and approval leaves a trail of who gave it.
en.blog.recibo-de-cobro-por-que-no-cuadra-c: Why what you collected never matches what reached the bank
Collections
Five reasons the month's receipts total and the bank deposit don't match. None of them is an arithmetic error.
The difference always has an explanation
You close the month, add up what you collected and compare it with what came into the accounts. It doesn't match. And because it's off by a little, the temptation is to adjust and move on.
The difference is hardly ever a calculation error. There are five specific causes, and each is handled differently.
The five causes

The cheque is collected but not deposited, or deposited and not credited. The receipt exists, the money doesn't yet. Until the bank credits it, that amount is in transit and has to be visible as such.
The bank fee. The customer paid 10,000 and 9,970 came in. The difference isn't a partial payment: it's an expense, and it goes to its own account.

The customer's withholding. In several countries the customer withholds a percentage and hands you a certificate. If it isn't recorded as a withholding, it looks like they underpaid and the invoice is left with a balance nobody will ever collect.
The exchange difference. You invoiced at one rate and collected at another. The difference is a result, not a mismatch. We cover it in where the margin gets lost.
A payment that reached the bank without a receipt. A transfer from a customer who didn't say. The money is there and nobody knows which invoice it's for: it ends up as an unidentified item that ages.
The common pattern

Looking at all five together, the pattern shows: in every one there's an amount that exists and isn't recorded as what it is. A fee booked as a partial payment, a withholding treated as non-payment, an exchange difference buried in revenue.
And they all produce the same end symptom: invoices with small balances that never close, and a customer who thinks they paid in full while your system says they owe 30.
Those tiny balances cost more than they look: they dirty the ageing report, send collectors chasing amounts that don't exist, and end up written off as bad debt having never been a debt at all.
What the system should do
Tell collection apart from deposit, with money in transit kept in plain sight.
Record fee, withholding and exchange difference as their own items, each to its own account.
Close the invoice when the sum of all those items covers the amount, not just the cash received.
Keep a tray of unidentified receipts, so a payment with no owner is visible instead of dissolving.
Let collected and deposited reconcile themselves
Zyntello separates collection from deposit, records fees and withholdings as what they are, and calculates the exchange difference at collection.
en.blog.orden-recepcion-factura-los-tres-do: Order, receipt and invoice: the three documents almost nobody matches
Purchasing control
You overpay because nobody matches what was ordered with what arrived and with what gets invoiced. The control is three-way, and it always fails at the same point.
Three moments, three documents, three figures
A purchase goes through three moments, and each produces its own document with its own figure:
What you ordered — the purchase order: agreed quantity and price.
What arrived — the goods receipt: what actually went into the warehouse.
What you're charged — the supplier's invoice.
When all three match, you pay without thinking. The control is not paying anything where the three don't match. It sounds obvious; almost nobody does it.
Where it always fails
The interesting part is that the failure is hardly ever in the invoice. It's in the middle:
Goods are received without checking against the order. The warehouse notes what arrived, without looking at whether it's what was ordered. If 95 of 100 arrived, the difference surfaces weeks later.
What's invoiced is what was ordered, not what was received. The supplier invoices the full order and nobody cross-checks it with the partial receipt.
The invoice price isn't the order price. An increase nobody authorised, and it gets paid because the invoice is already approved.
Goods arrive with no order. The hardest case: something turned up that nobody formally ordered, and now you have to decide whether to pay for it.
Returns to the supplier are the most neglected point: the goods go back, and if that isn't linked to its credit note, you end up paying the full invoice for something you no longer have.
Tolerances, which are what make the control usable
A control that blocks over a cent gets switched off within a week. That's why you need tolerances, and deciding them is part of the job:
A small quantity difference in bulk goods is normal; in equipment, it isn't.
A price difference within an agreed margin can go through; above it, it goes to approval.
And above all: what breaches the tolerance isn't blocked in silence. It goes to someone who decides, by name.
What you gain, beyond not overpaying
You know what you owe before the invoice arrives. Goods received and not invoiced are a real debt, and if they aren't recorded, your liabilities are incomplete.
Inventory cost is formed on receipt, not on invoicing, which is when it should be formed.
You measure the supplier with data: how long they really take, how often they deliver short. That feeds the reorder point.
Pay for what was ordered and arrived
Zyntello Purchasing matches order, receipt and invoice with the tolerances you define, and whatever falls outside goes to a named approver.
en.blog.retenciones-a-proveedores-que-descu: Supplier withholdings: the deduction that throws the supplier's account out
Payments
Withholding wrongly doesn't throw an error: it leaves the supplier claiming a balance you think you've paid. Why it happens and how to close it from the supplier record.
What it is and why it throws things out
When you pay certain suppliers you don't hand over the full amount: a part is withheld and paid to the tax authority on their behalf. The supplier gets a certificate for that withholding.

The mismatch appears when the withholding is recorded as if it were a smaller payment. Then the invoice is left with an outstanding balance that isn't owed, the supplier claims it, and someone ends up paying twice or leaving the balance there forever.

A withholding doesn't reduce what you owe the supplier: it moves it to the tax authority. The invoice is settled in full, part in cash and part in withholding. If the system has no such concept, there's no way to record it properly.
Where everyone gets it wrong
Withholding from the wrong party. The rate and the obligation depend on the type of supplier and the type of service. Applying it out of habit fails on the new cases.
The wrong rate is applied. There isn't just one: they change by category.
It's calculated on the wrong base. On the tax-inclusive total when it should have been on another base, or the other way round.
The certificate isn't issued. The supplier needs that document to credit what was withheld. Without it, the problem is theirs and yours.
It doesn't reach the return. What's withheld has to be declared. If it lives only on the invoice and not in the return, it's missing when you file.
It's fixed on the supplier, not on the payment
As with forms 606 and 607, the fix isn't where the problem shows up:
The supplier's type and tax regime are set once, when they're created.
The type of service goes on the document, and what to withhold follows from it.
The system proposes the withholding; the person confirms, doesn't calculate.
The certificate is issued with the payment, not as a separate errand someone has to remember.
The return is built from the recorded withholdings, not from a parallel spreadsheet.
The rates, bases and supplier types subject to withholding are set by each country's regulations and get updated. Confirm the ones in force with your accountant or the relevant authority.
Withhold properly, with no phantom balances
Zyntello Accounts Payable proposes the withholding from the supplier and the service, issues the certificate and feeds the return.

en.blog.costo-real-de-una-importacion.titul: The real cost of an import: everything that isn't on the supplier's invoice
en.blog.costo-real-de-una-importacion.resum: Freight, insurance, duties, storage, inland transport. If they aren't allocated onto the goods, you sell believing you're making money and the real margin is something else.
en.blog.costo-real-de-una-importacion.secci: The mistake you pay for while selling
The foreign supplier's invoice says a number. That number is not what the goods cost you, and treating it as if it were is one of the most expensive margin mistakes there is.
Between the supplier and your shelf there's a list of costs that, depending on the product and the origin, can add a very considerable percentage to the purchase price:
International freight and insurance.
Duties and other import charges.
Customs broker fees and documentation.
Storage, demurrage and handling at the port.
Inland transport to the warehouse.
When all of that is booked as the month's expense instead of allocated onto the goods, inventory is understated and every sale reports a margin that doesn't exist.
How to allocate, and why the basis matters
Allocation isn't trivial when a shipment carries different items. The usual bases:
By value. The expensive absorbs more. It's the sensible basis for insurance and for charges calculated on value.
By weight or volume. It's the sensible basis for freight: what takes up more space costs more to bring.
By units. Simple, and almost always wrong when the items are heterogeneous.

A container with light electronics and heavy tools allocated by value loads the freight onto the electronics, which hardly weigh anything. The result: one product artificially expensive and another artificially cheap, and wrong pricing decisions on both.
The practical answer is to allocate each cost by its own basis: freight by weight or volume, insurance and duties by value. A single basis for everything is easier and gives a worse cost.
The timing problem: the costs arrive later
The practical complication: the goods arrive and start selling before all the expense invoices are in. The customs broker's comes two weeks later; the port demurrage, a month later.

If you wait to have everything, you can't sell. If you receive with no costs, the cost is born wrong. The way out is to work with an estimated cost on receipt and adjust it as each real expense arrives, with the system recalculating what has already gone out.
And that's where the costing method matters: the later adjustment behaves differently under average cost than under FIFO.
What the system should solve
An import file that groups the purchase and all its expenses, with what's still outstanding in plain sight.
Allocation by the basis that fits each cost, not one basis for everything.
Receipt at an estimated cost and a later adjustment with nothing redone by hand.
The final cost visible by item and by shipment, so you can compare origins.
en.blog.costo-real-de-una-importacion.cierr: Knowing what it really cost you
Zyntello Purchasing keeps the import file with all its expenses, allocates them by each cost's own basis and adjusts the cost as the invoices arrive.
en.blog.diferencia-cambiaria-donde-se-pierd: Exchange differences: where the margin leaks without anyone seeing
Multi-currency
You invoice at one rate and collect at another. That difference is a result, not a reconciliation error — and if it dissolves into revenue, the margin you see isn't the real one.
The mechanism, in one sentence
If you invoice in one currency and collect in another, the rate moved between invoice and collection. That difference is money: gained or lost, depending on the direction.
It isn't an error, it isn't a mismatch, and it doesn't get corrected. It's a business result, like a discount or a finance cost, and it has to be visible as such.
The problem isn't that it exists: it's when it gets buried inside revenue. Then your sales margin rises and falls with the exchange rate, and stops telling you whether you sell well.
The rule that settles it all
Every document stores its amount AND its rate, and that rate is never recalculated. Everything else follows from that:
The invoice is worth what it was worth the day it was issued. Forever.
The payment is worth what it was worth the day it was collected.
The difference between the two goes to its own income-statement account.
The outstanding balance is valued at today's rate, which is why it changes even when the customer pays nothing.
A system that stores only an amount and converts on display rewrites the past: the invoice from six months ago changes figure every time you open it, and stops matching what the customer paid.
The four places it shows up
Collecting from a customer in a currency other than the invoice's.
Paying a supplier, the same thing in reverse: here the difference usually hurts more because it wasn't budgeted.
Valuing open balances at close. What you're owed and what you owe change value without anyone doing anything.
In foreign-currency bank accounts. The balance is worth something different every day.
The last two are the most forgotten, and they're the ones that make the balance sheet wrong without a single transaction being wrong.
Inventory is the special case
With inventory the rule changes, and getting it wrong is an expensive mistake: goods keep the cost at which they came in. They aren't revalued because the rate moved.

If it's revalued on every movement, each sale's margin turns into noise: two identical sales of the same item give different margins depending on the day. That makes it impossible to know which product is profitable.
The full reasoning is in average cost or FIFO, and the extreme case in invoicing in Venezuela.
Multi-currency end to end
In Zyntello every document carries its rate, the exchange difference goes to its own account and reports come out in any currency without rewriting the past.
en.blog.cierre-mensual-por-que-tarda-tres-s: Why the monthly close takes three weeks
Accounting close
The close isn't slow because of volume: it's slow because of what has to be rebuilt every month. When the numbers land on the 20th, they're no longer any use for deciding.
The real cost of a slow close
A close that finishes on the 20th isn't an accounting problem: it's a management problem. It means twenty days of deciding blind, on a feeling about how the month went instead of on the figure.
And it also means that when a problem appears — a margin that dropped, an expense that spiked — it's found seven weeks after it started.
Where the time actually goes
From what we've seen, the time doesn't go into bookkeeping. It goes into this:
Rebuilding what wasn't recorded at the time. Supplier invoices that arrived late, expenses paid on someone's card, a till nobody balanced.
Reconciling the banks by hand. Line by line, hunting for what each movement belongs to.
Squaring inventory with accounting. Two figures that should come from the same place and come from different ones.
Chasing whoever has to approve something. Provisions, adjustments, reclassifications waiting on an answer.
Redoing the same entries every month: depreciation, accruals, amortisation, provisions.
The pattern: nearly all the close's time goes on tasks that aren't the close's. They're the month's tasks that weren't done when they were due, and the close is where they pile up.
How to shorten it, in order of impact
Have every transaction post its own entry as it happens. A sale, a purchase, a payment and a stock movement post themselves. If the month has to be booked at the end, the close is the whole month.
Assisted reconciliation. Let the system propose the match and the person confirm. It's the task that eats the most hours and the easiest to automate.
Scheduled recurring entries. Depreciation and accruals should never be typed by hand.
A real cut-off date. A day after which nothing else is recorded in the period. Without a cut-off, the close is a moving target.
Approvals with a deadline. Keep what's pending in plain sight, with who's holding it, instead of in an email chain.
The sign you're on track
There's a simple check: could you produce a reasonable income statement on the 2nd? Not final — reasonable, with provisions estimated.

If the answer is no because data is missing, the problem is in the daily recording. If it's no because things still need booking, the problem is that accounting trails the operation instead of coming out of it.
Close in days, not weeks
In Zyntello every transaction posts its entry as it happens, reconciliation is assisted and recurring entries are scheduled. The close stops being a reconstruction.
en.blog.centros-de-costo-que-nadie-usa.titu: Cost centres: why they get set up and then nobody uses them
en.blog.centros-de-costo-que-nadie-usa.resu: They go up with enthusiasm at go-live and three months later half the expenses land in «general». Why it happens and how to make them survive.
en.blog.centros-de-costo-que-nadie-usa.secc: It's one of the most repeated stories in any rollout: cost centres get defined by branch, by department or by project, carefully configured… and three months later most expenses go to a generic one.
When that happens, the cost-centre report doesn't just stop being useful: it misleads. It shows a cheap department because its expenses ended up somewhere else.
There are too many. Whoever keys an invoice has to pick from forty options. They pick the first one or the generic one.

Nobody knows which one applies. A maintenance expense at a branch — does it go to the branch or to maintenance? If it isn't written down, each person decides differently and the report mixes criteria.
They aren't mandatory. The field can be left empty, so it is.
Nobody looks at the report. And what nobody looks at stops being filled in. It's the root cause behind nearly all the others.
Some expenses belong to several at once — rent, electricity — and there's no allocation rule, so they go whole to one or to none.
Start with few. Five that get used are worth more than forty filled in at random. You can open more once the five work.
Let them propose themselves. The cost centre is inferred from the supplier, the expense type or who requested it. The person confirms, doesn't choose.
Mandatory where it matters. Not everywhere: on the expense accounts where the analysis is worth something.
Automatic allocation for shared ones. Rent is split by a fixed rule — square metres, headcount, revenue — defined once.
Have someone look at the report every month, visibly. If a centre's owner receives their spend and answers for it, the data cleans itself.
The check that tells you whether they're alive: what percentage of last quarter's spend went to the generic centre. Above a third, cost-centre analysis can't be used to decide anything.
en.blog.centros-de-costo-que-nadie-usa.cier: In Zyntello the cost centre is proposed from the document and can be required where it matters, with automatic allocation for shared expenses.
en.blog.por-que-fracasan-las-implantaciones: Why ERP rollouts fail (and it's hardly ever the software)
Rollout
The six real reasons an ERP gets abandoned. None of them appears in a feature comparison, and all of them can be prevented.
A missing feature is hardly ever it
When a company abandons its ERP, the explanation given is usually «it didn't work». But when you ask in detail, a feature is hardly ever missing: what's missing is anyone using it properly.
Twenty years of watching this up close gives a fairly clear pattern, and it's six causes.
The six causes
The project outlasted everyone's patience. Eighteen months of rollout is long enough for the business, the team and the sponsor to change. What's delivered at the end is no longer what was asked for.
Nobody taught what each screen was for. The training covered which buttons to press, not which decision each piece of data supports. The result: fields filled in just to get past them.
Dirty data got migrated. Duplicate customers, items at zero cost, balances that didn't add up. The new system inherits the problem and takes the blame.
The old process was replicated. The ERP was configured to do exactly what was done before, workarounds included. Then it adds nothing, only steps.
Nobody owned it. The project belonged to IT, and IT can't decide how a purchase gets approved.
The vendor vanished at go-live. The real problems show up three months in, when the first close and the first odd case arrive.
The most underrated cause is the second one. A screen the user doesn't understand is filled in wrongly from day one, and from then on every report that uses it is wrong — with nothing failing.
What does work
Start with one module, not everything. The one that hurts most. Live in weeks, not quarters.
Clean the data before, not during. It's boring work and it's what decides whether the new system is born trustworthy.
Review the process before configuring it. If approval happens on WhatsApp today, automating that is automating the mess.
An owner from the business, not from IT. Someone who can decide how things get done.
Help inside the screen. So whoever hesitates finds the answer where the field is, not in a manual nobody opens.
If you're at the choosing stage, it's worth reading the awkward questions worth asking before you sign.
An ERP you start with one piece
Zyntello is bought module by module: you start with whichever hurts today and add the rest on top of the same data, with no year-long project.
en.blog.como-elegir-un-erp-preguntas-incomo: The awkward questions worth asking before you sign for an ERP
Choosing a system
Ten questions no salesperson offers, and that separate a system that will serve you from one you'll abandon in two years.
The demo always goes well
Every demo works. It's rehearsed, on clean data, following the happy path. That's why comparing demos distinguishes almost nothing.
What does distinguish is asking about what the demo doesn't show: the data, the failure, the exit and the after.
About your data
Can I export everything, whenever I want, without asking permission? And in what format. The answer to this says a lot about the whole relationship.
If I stop being a customer, what happens to my information? There should be a written procedure, not a promise.
Who can see my data from the inside? And if you run several companies: how do you guarantee that one company's data isn't visible from another?
How often are backups taken and how are they restored? Ask them to tell you about the last time they actually restored one.
About when something goes wrong
What happens if the internet goes down mid-invoicing? Especially with e-invoicing: can I keep selling?
Show me the screen of documents pending submission. The most revealing request: if it doesn't exist, the backlogs will be invisible.
What response commitment do I have in writing? A published service level agreement, not an intention.
Who do I talk to when something breaks? Someone who knows my case, or a generic queue?
About money and the future
What is NOT included in the price? It's a better question than what is. Rollout, migration, training, support, upgrades.
What happens when the tax law changes? Is it part of the subscription or does an adaptation invoice arrive?
If I grow to three companies or another country, what changes? In price and in work.
Is there a lock-in period? And if so, why. A product that retains with clauses isn't retaining with product.
One request worth ten questions: «show me a customer like me, operating, not a demo». If there's no way to see the system doing your case at real volume, that's already an answer.
Ask us these questions
All of them. The answers are published: the SLA, the data policy, the deletion procedure and the per-module pricing.

en.blog.multiempresa-de-verdad-o-de-mentira: Real multi-company: what to ask if you have more than one entity
Architecture
Almost every system claims to support multiple companies. The gap between saying it and doing it shows up in four specific questions.
Two very different things with the same name
«Multi-company» means two completely different things depending on who says it:
Several separate installations. Each company its own database, login and configuration. It works, but every change is made as many times as you have companies, and consolidating means a spreadsheet.
A system that understands there are several companies. Data separated where it must be, shared where it makes sense, and one place to work.
The second is considerably harder to build, which is why the first gets sold under the same name.
The four questions that tell them apart

Is a customer who buys from two of my companies stored twice? If they have to be created in each one, every correction has to be made twice, and one copy with a wrong tax ID is enough for those invoices to go out wrong.
Can I switch company without logging in again? It looks like convenience and it's more than that: it tells you whether the system understands the concept or whether these are disguised installations.
Are permissions per company? Someone may need to see everything in one and nothing in another. If permissions are global, they either see everything or nothing.
Can I consolidate without exporting? See the whole without building a separate sheet every month.

And a fifth, the one that really matters: ask to see any screen — a customer list, a sales report — with two companies loaded. If anything from the other company shows up, even a name in a dropdown, that's a leak. In a system built properly it never happens.
What's shared and what isn't
The right line isn't «everything separate». There are things where sharing is the sensible answer:
Shared: the customer and supplier catalogue with their tax ID — a tax number doesn't change depending on which of your companies is invoicing — plus countries and currencies.
NEVER shared: the accounting, document numbering, balances, inventory, payroll, permissions and any operational data.
Getting that line wrong in either direction causes problems: over-sharing is a leak; over-separating forces you to maintain the same data in several places, and then they diverge.
Several companies, one system
Zyntello separates accounting, numbering, balances and permissions by company, and shares what should be shared. With no extra cost per company.
en.blog.multimoneda-no-es-un-campo.titulo: Multi-currency isn't a field: it's the whole journey
en.blog.multimoneda-no-es-un-campo.resumen: Having a currency dropdown isn't being multi-currency. The test is in the collection, in the close and in the report from six months ago.
en.blog.multimoneda-no-es-un-campo.seccione: The field is the easy part
Adding a currency dropdown to an invoice is half an hour's work. That's why almost every system claims to be multi-currency.
The hard part is everything else: having that data survive the collection, the close, the report and the passing of time without contradicting itself.
Invoice in one currency, collect in another. Does the system calculate the exchange difference and send it to its own account, or leave you an unbalanced amount that someone adjusts by hand?
Open a document from six months ago. Does it show the figure invoiced back then, or convert it at today's rate? If it converts, it's rewriting the past.
Look at inventory. Does it keep the cost at which the goods came in, or revalue it? Revaluing it turns the margin into noise.
Ask for a balance sheet in the other currency. Does it come out, and can you explain where each conversion came from?

A system that fails the second test is the most dangerous, because it throws no error: the historical reports simply change figure depending on the day you look at them, and nobody knows which one was right.
Where it matters more than it looks
Plenty of people think this only applies if you invoice abroad. It doesn't:
If you buy imported and sell locally, your cost is multi-currency even if your invoices aren't.
If you hold a foreign-currency bank account, its balance changes value every day.
If you pay a foreign supplier on terms, the debt changes value while it's unpaid.
The full mechanism is in exchange differences, and the most demanding case in invoicing in Venezuela.

en.blog.que-comprueba-la-dgii-en-un-ncf.tit: What the DGII actually checks in an NCF
en.blog.que-comprueba-la-dgii-en-un-ncf.res: An NCF gets rejected for what you can't see: the sequence used up, a type that doesn't match the customer, a date outside the authorisation. How to avoid it.
en.blog.que-comprueba-la-dgii-en-un-ncf.sec: The receipt looks right and still gets rejected

The NCF (Número de Comprobante Fiscal) is what turns an invoice into a document with tax value in the Dominican Republic. And the part that surprises almost everyone starting out is that an invoice can be issued perfectly — right amounts, right customer, ITBIS calculated — and still be useless.

The reason is that an NCF isn't a number you pick: it's a sequence authorised by the DGII, with a type, a range and an expiry date. When any of those three doesn't fit, the receipt stops being valid for the customer to use, and that's found out late: when the customer reports it in their 606 and it doesn't match.

The symptom of a badly issued NCF isn't an error on screen. It's a call from the customer three months later saying their accountant can't use your invoice. By then you have to void and reissue, with the tax period already closed.
The three things that have to line up
A valid receipt needs the type, the sequence and the validity period to line up at the same time:

The type has to match the customer. A tax-credit receipt (type 01) is for a customer with an RNC who will use it to deduct. A final-consumer one (02) is for someone who won't. Issuing an 02 to a company throws no error, but it takes away the customer's right to deduct the ITBIS.
The sequence has to be inside the authorised range. Each range has a start and an end number. When it runs out, you can't keep numbering: you have to request a new one.
The date has to be inside the validity period. Ranges expire. An NCF issued after its authorisation's expiry date is worthless, even if the number is inside the range.
And there's a fourth that isn't the DGII's but breaks things just the same: the sequence can't repeat or skip. A number used twice is a serious problem, and a gap has to be explainable.
The types most often confused
Most of the rejections we've seen come from choosing the wrong type, not from a numbering fault:
01 · Tax credit. A customer with an RNC who will deduct the ITBIS. It requires the customer's RNC, and that it be correct.
02 · Final consumer. An individual who doesn't deduct. If you issue it to a company, that company can't use it.
03 · Debit note and 04 · Credit note. They amend an earlier receipt and have to reference it. A credit note without the NCF it corrects is orphaned.
11 · Purchases. The buyer issues it when buying from someone who can't issue a receipt. It's the most forgotten one.
14 · Special regime and 15 · Government. For customers under a particular regime; using an 01 with them usually ends in rejection.
The practical rule: the type is decided by who the customer is, not by what you sell them. That's the most repeated mistake.
What fails in practice
After rolling out invoicing in quite a few Dominican companies, the problems repeat with striking regularity:
The sequence runs out on a Friday afternoon. Nobody watches how many are left until none are, and then you can't invoice. A warning at 80% solves 90% of these scares.

Two points of sale share a range. If two tills take numbers from the same range without coordinating, sooner or later they issue the same one. The number has to come from a single place that knows which was the last.
The customer's RNC is mistyped. One digit wrong and the receipt is useless for deducting. Validating the RNC against the official register when you create the customer avoids the whole problem.
Voiding is done wrong. An issued receipt isn't deleted: it's voided and reported as voided. Deleting it from the database leaves a gap in the sequence that you then have to explain.
How to prevent it before issuing
All of this is checkable before the invoice exists, and that's where a system really earns its keep. What should happen when you press «Invoice»:
The type proposes itself, based on whether the customer has an RNC and on their regime.
The number comes from the authorised sequence, from a single source, with no way to repeat even if three tills invoice at once.
The range's validity is checked against the document's date, not today's.
You're warned when few receipts are left, with time to request the new authorisation.
Voiding leaves the receipt voided and reportable; it never deletes it.

None of these checks is hard. What's hard is remembering to do them by hand every time, with the customer waiting at the counter. And if you're already on e-invoicing with e-CF, there's even less room to improvise.
Tax rules change. This article explains how things work in general as of September 2026; for a specific case, always confirm with the DGII or your accountant.

en.blog.ecf-facturacion-electronica-dominic: e-CF: what really changes with e-invoicing in the Dominican Republic
E-invoicing
An e-CF isn't «the NCF as a PDF». It changes who validates, when, and what happens if the DGII doesn't answer. What you need ready before the deadline.
The starting mistake: thinking it's the same paper, digitised
The costliest confusion we see is this one: thinking the Electronic Tax Receipt is the usual invoice, just emailed. It isn't. It changes who decides whether the invoice exists.

With the traditional NCF, you issue and the DGII finds out later, in your returns. With the e-CF, the document is a digitally signed XML that is sent to the DGII and waits for its answer. Until there's an answer, there's no valid receipt.

That difference changes everything at the counter: where a technical problem used to leave you unable to print, now it can leave you unable to invoice. That's why the rollout isn't «installing a program»: it's reviewing what happens in your operation when the link to the DGII doesn't answer.
The pieces you need in place first
You can't start on the deadline day. What you need:
A digital certificate. It's what signs the documents. An authorised certification body issues it, it takes time to obtain and it expires: note its expiry date the way you note an insurance policy's.
Your customer data, complete and correct. The XML carries the RNC and the registered name. What gets through today because «the accountant fixes it» is rejected there by a machine.
Your catalogue properly classified. Every line carries its tax classification. An item wrongly flagged as exempt turns into a repeated rejection.
An answer for the failure. What the cashier does if there's no internet or the DGII doesn't answer. This is decided beforehand, not on the spot.
The part nobody plans for: when it fails
This is the conversation most often postponed and the one that costs the most money. An e-invoicing system has to answer three questions:
Can you keep selling? The operational answer has to be yes. If you can't, every outage is a closed shop.
What do you hand the customer meanwhile? It has to be something that can later become the final receipt, without re-keying the sale.
Who resends what's pending and how do you know it was resent? If the pending queue isn't in plain sight, you find out at month end that there are documents that never arrived.

The queue of unsent documents is the most important screen in an e-invoicing system, and the one almost no demo shows. A stuck document throws no error at the point of sale: the sale goes through, the customer leaves, and the receipt doesn't exist for the tax authority.
What does get better
It isn't all burden. Set up well, the e-CF solves problems that used to be chronic:
No more exhausted ranges. Numbering stops depending on an authorised booklet that runs out on a Friday.
The customer gets the receipt immediately, not when someone comes by to collect it.
Returns are built from exactly what was sent, not from a separate entry. Reconciling stops being a month-end job.
Credit notes stay linked to the document they correct, without depending on someone typing the reference correctly.
If you're still on traditional NCFs, it's worth reading what the DGII checks in an NCF: almost everything that fails for you there today will fail faster electronically.

The mandatory timetable goes by taxpayer size and has been adjusted over time. Confirm which group you're in and on what date directly with the DGII or your accountant: that's the fact that decides how much of a hurry you're in.
Is the e-CF coming for you and you don't know where to start?
We'll tell you what you're actually missing — data, catalogue, certificate — before the deadline squeezes you.

en.blog.factura-electronica-colombia-dian.t: E-invoicing in Colombia: what the DIAN validates before the sale exists
en.blog.factura-electronica-colombia-dian.r: In Colombia the DIAN validates FIRST: no validation, no invoice. What the CUFE is, why a document gets rejected and what else you have to issue.
en.blog.factura-electronica-colombia-dian.s: The difference that changes everything: validation comes first

Colombia has one of the strictest models in the region: pre-validation. The electronic sales invoice is transmitted to the DIAN and is only valid once the DIAN validates it. It isn't an informational filing: it's a permission.

In practice that means your system doesn't create the invoice: the DIAN creates it by accepting it. And that's why the document carries the CUFE, the unique code identifying that specific invoice and letting anyone verify it exists.
If you come from a country where you invoice and report afterwards, this is the shift in mindset: here a data error isn't a later correction, it's a sale you can't document on the spot.
Why the DIAN rejects a document
Rejections are hardly ever about the amount. They're about the detail nobody checks:
Buyer data incomplete or malformed. A NIT with the wrong check digit, the person type set wrong, a tax responsibility that doesn't apply.
Numbering outside the current resolution. The prefix and range are authorised by resolution, with a validity period. Outside that, there's no invoice.
Taxes that don't match the base. VAT calculated on a base different from the one declared, or an exempt item carrying tax.
Invalid units of measure. The standard requires specific codes; «unit» typed by hand isn't one.
The practical consequence: the quality of your customer master stops being an admin matter and becomes an operational one. A badly captured customer is an invoice that doesn't go out.
It isn't just the sales invoice
The commonest scoping mistake is preparing only the sales invoice. The Colombian system covers more:
Electronic credit and debit notes, which reference the invoice they correct.
Supporting document for purchases from those not required to invoice electronically. If you buy from someone not obliged, you issue the document.
Electronic payroll, which is a separate filing, with its own periodicity, and which usually catches out anyone who thought this was only about invoicing.
Buyer events — acknowledgement of receipt, acceptance — which in certain cases are what let the invoice circulate as a negotiable instrument.
If you'll be running payroll too, it's worth looking at how payroll is calculated in Colombia, because the electronic filing feeds off that calculation: if the calculation is wrong, so is the filing.
If you operate in several countries at once

Here's the problem almost nobody anticipates: tax rules aren't configured, they're implemented. Colombia validates first, the Dominican Republic has its own scheme, Guatemala works through certifiers and Costa Rica with its own format and receiver acceptance. They aren't variants of the same thing.

A system that says «multi-country supported» can mean two very different things: that it really has the four regimes implemented, or that it has a field where you type the tax's name. The question that tells them apart: show me an invoice issued and validated in each country.

Colombian rules are updated by resolution fairly often and there are deadlines that depend on your activity and size. Confirm your specific case with the DIAN or your accountant before making calendar decisions.

en.blog.fel-guatemala-factura-electronica-e: FEL in Guatemala: the certifier, the DTE and what breaks when you switch
E-invoicing
In Guatemala there's a middle piece that doesn't exist elsewhere: the certifier. What that means, what data the DTE requires and where migration fails.
The piece that doesn't exist elsewhere

Guatemala's online e-invoicing regime introduces an actor that surprises outsiders: the certifier. Your system doesn't talk directly to the SAT; it talks to an authorised certifier, which certifies the document and registers it.

That has an immediate practical consequence: you pick a provider, and that choice ties you in. The document format is the same, but the integration isn't. Changing certifier isn't changing a key: it's rebuilding the connection.

Before signing with a certifier, ask what happens if you want to leave: whether you take the history, in what format, and how long cancelling takes. It's the conversation nobody has at the start and everybody ends up having.
The DTE and what it requires
The DTE (Documento Tributario Electrónico) is the document itself, and once certified it's uniquely identified. What has to be in order for it to go out:
The recipient's NIT, valid. For a final consumer there's a specific way to state it; getting it wrong turns an ordinary sale into a questionable document.
The right document type. Invoice, credit note, debit note and the special types by activity. Each with its own rules.
Taxes properly classified. Besides VAT, some activities carry specific taxes that are flagged separately.
The mandatory wording for your regime. A document missing the legend it should carry can be incomplete even if the numbers are perfect.
Where migration breaks
From what we've seen accompanying migrations, this is what really costs:
The customer master. Years of NITs typed by eye, with spaces, dashes and the odd «CF» written six different ways. You clean it beforehand or you clean it with the customer waiting.
Counter sales. Where you used to invoice fast and fix it later, now you have to get it right first time.
Voiding. Voiding a DTE has its rules and deadlines; it isn't deleting a line. Whoever doesn't internalise that piles up documents they should have voided and now can't.
History. What was issued before still exists and has to stay consultable. A new system that doesn't take the past along leaves the company with two places to look.
What to demand of a system here
With FEL now generally mandatory, the question isn't whether it issues: it's how it behaves when something goes wrong.
The queue of documents pending certification should be in plain sight, not buried in a log.
You should be able to keep selling if the certifier doesn't answer, and what's pending should recover by itself.
The NIT should be validated when you create the customer, not when you issue.
Voids should respect the deadline and warn before it passes.
This article describes how things work in general as of September 2026. Your specific obligations depend on your regime and activity: confirm them with the SAT or your accountant.

en.blog.factura-electronica-costa-rica-haci: Costa Rica: the numeric key, the consecutive number and the recipient's response
E-invoicing
In Costa Rica the receipt doesn't end when you send it: the recipient responds. What the numeric key is, why the consecutive number can't be improvised and what happens if you don't accept.
Two numbers people confuse
The Costa Rican system works with two different identifiers, and mixing them is the source of a good share of the problems:
The numeric key identifies the receipt uniquely at national level. It's built following a fixed structure, and any deviation invalidates it.
The consecutive number is your own numbering: it carries the branch, the terminal and the document type. It's yours, but its format is defined.
The consequence: neither of them can be «made up» or reassigned. If your system lets you edit either by hand, sooner or later you'll have two documents fighting over the same number.
What almost nobody sets up: the recipient's response
Here's the quirk most often overlooked. In Costa Rica it isn't enough for you to issue: when you receive a document, you're expected to respond — accepting it, partially accepting it or rejecting it.

And that turns what looked like a sales task into a purchasing one. If your supplier invoices you something you didn't order, or at the wrong price, the answer isn't a phone call: it's a documented rejection.
Companies that only set up the issuing side discover this months later, with a pile of received documents left unanswered. There's no error to warn you: it simply wasn't done.
The format changes, and changing it isn't optional
The document schema has evolved through versions, and each version change has a date after which the previous one stops being accepted. It's recurring maintenance, not an installation.

That's something to ask before choosing a system: who updates the format when the tax ministry publishes a new version, and whether that's in the subscription or billed separately. In a system that doesn't update it, the change date is the day you stop being able to invoice.
What's worth having sorted
The recipient's ID, validated on entry. Individual ID, company ID, DIMEX or NITE have different formats and aren't interchangeable.
Consecutive numbers per branch and terminal, coming from a single source, even if several points invoice at once.
An inbox of received documents, with the unanswered ones in plain sight.
A queue of pending submissions, so an outage doesn't turn into documents that never arrived.
Format versions and deadlines are published by the tax ministry and updated periodically. Confirm the current version and your specific obligations with the ministry or your accountant.

en.blog.facturacion-venezuela-iva-igtf.titu: Venezuela: invoicing in two currencies, with VAT and IGTF, without losing the margin
en.blog.facturacion-venezuela-iva-igtf.resu: Invoicing in Venezuela isn't a tax problem: it's an exchange-rate problem. Which rate governs each document and why the margin disappears between the sale and the payment.
en.blog.facturacion-venezuela-iva-igtf.secc: The problem isn't the tax: it's the rate

Anyone who's never operated in Venezuela assumes the hard part is the tax regime. Anyone who does operate there knows the hard part is something else: between selling and collecting, the value of what you invoiced changed.

That turns a decision which elsewhere is an accounting one — which rate to apply — into a business decision taken several times a day. And if the system doesn't take it well, the margin vanishes without any report saying so: the sale looks right, the payment looks right, and the difference was eaten by the rate.
The symptom is a company that sells at a margin on paper and has no money in the bank. There's no error anywhere: there's a rate applied at the wrong moment.
Which rate governs at each moment
The rule that avoids most mismatches is being clear that a document is valued at the rate of ITS date, not today's. It sounds obvious and it's exactly what almost no system gets right:
The invoice carries the rate of the day it was issued. That one is never touched again.
The payment carries the rate of the day it was collected. If it's different, the difference is a result, not an error to correct.
The outstanding balance is valued at the rate of the moment you look at it, which is why it changes even if the customer has paid nothing.
Inventory keeps the cost at which it came in. Revaluing it with every rate move turns the margin into noise.

A system that stores only the amount in one currency and converts on display is doomed to lie: it rewrites the past every time the rate moves. The amount and its rate travel together, on the document, forever.
VAT and the transactions tax

On top of that come the country's own obligations. VAT with its rate and its withholdings by taxpayer type, and the tax on large financial transactions, which charges certain payments — notably those made in foreign currency — and which in practice changes the final amount collected depending on how you're paid.

That last one breaks more systems than anything: the invoice total and the payment total don't match, and not because of an error. The system has to know how to calculate it and record it separately, not buried inside the price.

Rates, withholding percentages and the IGTF's scope are modified by administrative ruling and have changed several times. Confirm the current ones with the SENIAT or your accountant: what's explained here is the mechanism, not the numbers.
What to demand of a system for Venezuela
Every document should store its own rate, and that rate must not be recalculable later.
The gap between the invoice's rate and the payment's should come out as an exchange difference, with its own account, not diluted into revenue.
The IGTF should be calculated and recorded separately, not added into the price.
Reports should be viewable in both currencies without redoing the calculations by hand.
If you operate in several countries, the same reasoning applies to any currency: we explain it in more detail in where the margin leaks with exchange differences.

en.blog.formatos-606-607-dgii-que-los-descu: Forms 606 and 607: why they never balance first time
Tax returns
The 606 and the 607 don't fail on the total: they fail on the detail. The six causes that cost a whole day every month, and how to prevent them at data entry.
The monthly ritual that shouldn't exist

In many Dominican companies there's one day a month devoted to balancing the 606 and the 607. You export, it doesn't balance, you review line by line, you fix by hand and you file. Next month, the same.
What's striking is that almost none of the causes is in the return. They're in the data entry, weeks earlier. The return is just where they become visible.
The six causes, in order of frequency
The supplier's RNC is wrong or missing. One digit off and the line doesn't cross-match what the supplier reported.
The type of good or service is misclassified. It's a field filled in out of habit when the supplier is created and nobody reviews afterwards.
The withholding wasn't applied where it should have been. Or it was applied where it shouldn't. Both throw things out, in opposite directions.
The purchase's NCF wasn't captured. The invoice was paid, the expense was booked, and the receipt number stayed on the paper.
The document date and the period date don't match. A month-end invoice entered on the 2nd ends up in the wrong period.
There are voided receipts still showing as valid, or deleted ones that should appear as voided.
It's fixed at data entry, not in the return
The practical conclusion: every fix you make in the 606 spreadsheet is a validation that was missing three weeks earlier. As long as the fix lives in the return, next month it comes back.
What does close it:
The RNC is validated against the official register when the supplier is created, not when you file.
The type of good or service is mandatory on the supplier, and the document inherits it.
The withholding proposes itself from the supplier and service type, instead of being remembered.
You can't record a purchase with a tax receipt without its NCF.
The period is decided by the document's date, not the entry date.
It's the same principle as with sales NCFs: what isn't validated at entry gets paid for at filing.
The forms and their fields are defined by the DGII and get updated. Confirm the current structure with the DGII or your accountant before automating anything.
Let the 606 balance without that monthly day
In Zyntello returns are built from what's already entered and validated, not from a spreadsheet someone assembles and corrects. You get that day of the month back.

Why inventory never matches
Inventory control
The gap between the system and the shelf is hardly ever theft: it's six specific, fixable causes, and none of them throws an error message.
It's hardly ever theft

When the physical count doesn't match the system, the first suspicion is usually that stock is missing. Sometimes that's true. But in most cases we've seen, the stock is there: what fails is the record.
And the record fails for specific, repeated reasons, not bad luck. What follows are the six that show up again and again.
The six causes

The goods arrived before the paperwork. The truck came, it was unloaded and it went on the shelf. The supplier's invoice was entered three days later. In between, the system says one thing and the warehouse another — and those days' sales come out of stock the system doesn't know exists.
Sold without deducting. A sale that generates no stock movement. It happens with invoices raised outside the system and with modules that aren't connected to each other.

The unit of measure changed along the way. You buy by the case and sell by the unit. If the conversion isn't set up right, the error literally multiplies: a case of 24 deducted as one unit leaves 23 phantoms.
Returns don't come back. The customer returns something, the credit note is raised, and the goods sit in a corner without re-entering the system.
Shrinkage isn't recorded. What breaks, what expires, what's used internally. If it isn't written off, the system keeps counting it for months.
Transfers are left half done. It left one warehouse and the receipt at the other never got recorded. It's in the company, but for the system it's nowhere.
And then there's cost, which is the real problem
Being out on quantities is annoying. Being out on cost is what takes the margin with it, and it's far less visible.

If an item's cost is wrong, every sale of that item reports a wrong margin. No error, no warning: the profitability report says something untrue. Decisions get made on it — what to promote, what to drop, who to buy from — and they're made wrongly. We go into it in average cost or FIFO.

A stock adjustment corrects the QUANTITY, not the cost. If you bring in 10 missing units, they come in at the cost the system already had. When it's the cost that's wrong, adjusting quantities doesn't fix it and covers it up as well.
How to fix it, in order
The usual mistake is to start with the count. Counting a warehouse whose processes are still broken gives an exact number that's wrong again in two weeks. The order that works is:
First, close off unrecorded movements in and out. So nothing leaves without a document and receipts get recorded on receipt, not on invoicing.
Second, fix the unit conversions. It's a short job and it eliminates a whole class of errors.
Third, count. Now yes, and the count is what you adjust from.
Fourth, cycle counts. Not one full stocktake a year, which also means shutting down. A few items every week, starting with the fastest-moving and most valuable.
What doesn't work is the reverse: count first and promise that from now on everything will be recorded. That was already promised last year.
An inventory that does match

en.blog.costo-promedio-o-peps-cual-usar.tit: Average cost or FIFO: which to use, and why almost nobody can switch later
en.blog.costo-promedio-o-peps-cual-usar.res: The decision looks like an accounting one and it's a business one: it changes the margin you see, the value of inventory and what you declare. And changing it later rewrites history.
en.blog.costo-promedio-o-peps-cual-usar.sec: The question almost nobody asks at the start
You buy the same item three times at three different prices. You sell one unit. What did that unit cost you?
There's no single answer, which is why costing methods exist. The two most used in the region:
Average cost. Each receipt recalculates a weighted average, and issues go out at that average. It smooths the ups and downs.
FIFO (first in, first out). What goes out is the oldest, at its original cost. The stock that remains is valued at the most recent prices.
With stable prices it hardly matters. With prices that move — which is normal in imports or with exchange rates — the difference in the reported margin is large.
What really changes when you pick one
The margin you see on each sale. With prices rising, the average gives a cost lower than the last purchase price, so the margin looks better than replacing the item will be.
The value of inventory on the balance sheet. FIFO leaves stock valued at recent prices; the average, at a blend.
What you declare. Cost of sales changes, and with it the result.
Pricing decisions. Setting the sale price on an old average cost while prices are rising is like selling at last year's price.

The most practical risk of the average in a rising market: you sell at a positive accounting margin and it isn't enough to replace the same unit. The report says you made money; the till says you didn't.
Why switching later is so expensive
Here's the surprising part: a costing method isn't a switch. Changing it forces you either to recalculate history or to cut at a date, and either one breaks the comparability of your reports.
What's more, in many accounting frameworks the policy has to be kept over time and a change has to be justified. It isn't something you decide on a Tuesday because the numbers look nicer.
The practical recommendation: decide it at go-live, in writing, with the accountant present — not the day someone notices the margin doesn't add up.
What breaks either of them
The method doesn't matter if the input data is wrong. What invalidates costing, whichever it is:
Receiving with no cost. A receipt at zero poisons the average forever and throws no error.
Leaving import costs out. Freight, insurance and duties are part of the cost, not a separate expense. We cover it in the real cost of an import.
Adjusting quantities to paper over a cost problem. An adjustment keeps the cost: it fixes nothing and hides the cause.
Entering the supplier's invoice at a price different from the receipt's without the system recognising the difference.

en.blog.lotes-y-vencimientos-cuando-hacen-f: Batches and expiry dates: when you really need them and what it costs not to have them
Traceability
Tracking batches is work and not everyone needs it. But when you need it and it isn't there, the cost isn't operational: it's a product recall you can't narrow down.
When you need it and when it's overhead
Tracking batches means identifying every receipt and choosing which batch each issue comes from. It's real work in the warehouse, and it doesn't always pay off.
You need it when any of these apply:
The product expires — food, pharmacy, chemicals, cosmetics.
You need to be able to recall a specific group without recalling everything.
Sector regulations require traceability through to the end customer.
The supplier handles warranties by batch, or defects come in clusters.
If none of them applies, tracking them just in case only adds steps in the warehouse.
What it costs not to have them, when you needed them
The cost doesn't show up until the day of the problem, and then it shows up in full:
A recall you can't narrow down. If you don't know which units came from that batch, you recall the whole product and notify every customer.
Expired goods found on the shelf. With no date in the system, nobody warns in advance; the customer or the count finds it.
You can't sell in expiry order. What's at the front goes out, and what's behind it expires.
The claim against the supplier is impossible to sustain without being able to show which delivery the faulty goods came from.

The case that convinces everyone: a customer calls about a product in bad condition. With batches, you know which other units from that delivery went out and to whom. Without batches, the honest answer is «I don't know».
What has to be solved for it to be used
Traceability gets abandoned when it gets in the way. What decides whether it stays alive:
Capture the batch on receipt, by scanning a code if possible, not by typing.
When selling, have the system propose the right batch — the one closest to expiry — instead of asking.
Warn about what's about to expire with time to move it, not once it already has.
From a batch you can see which customers it went to, and from a sale, which batch it came from. Both ways.
And one detail that gets overlooked: batches go into the count too. Counting 40 units without knowing which batches leaves inventory balanced in total and out of balance in detail.
Traceability that doesn't get in the way

en.blog.punto-de-reorden-cuando-volver-a-pe: When to reorder: the calculation that avoids both stockouts and overbuying
Replenishment
Buying when you run out is too late. The reorder point isn't a fixed figure: it depends on how much you sell, how long the supplier takes and how much both of those vary.
Both mistakes cost the same
Running out and overbuying look like opposite problems, and both come from the same thing: not knowing when to order.
Running out is a lost sale and, sometimes, a customer who discovers the competitor did have it.
Overbuying is money sitting on a shelf, at risk of expiring or becoming obsolete.
The company that buys «when it looks low» usually has both at once: too much of what moves slowly and too little of what moves fast.
The calculation, no mystery
The reorder point is the quantity at which you place the order so it arrives before you run out. It's built from three things:
How much you sell a day of that item, measured over a representative period.
How long the supplier takes from ordering until the goods are available to sell. Not from dispatch: from when you can sell it.
How much both of them vary. That margin is the safety stock, and it's what absorbs the week you sold double or the supplier was late.
The important one is the third: with no safety margin, the reorder point is right half the time, which is exactly what happens when you calculate with clean averages.
The details that spoil it
The supplier's lead time isn't the one the supplier quotes. It's the one you measure: order date against availability date, over the last real orders.
Seasonal items can't be calculated on the annual average. A seasonal product's average describes no month of the year.
Promotions break the calculation. A campaign multiplies demand; if the reorder point doesn't know, it sells out in two days.
The supplier's minimum rules. There's little point calculating that you need 7 if the supplier sells cases of 24.

A replenishment system born with every threshold at zero warns about nothing, and looks like it works: it throws no errors, it simply never suggests buying. Thresholds have to be set item by item, or at least by family.
Before the calculation, the data
None of this works if inventory doesn't match. A reorder point calculated on wrong stock levels suggests buying what you already have too much of and doesn't suggest what you're short of.
That's why the order is: first make inventory match, then automate replenishment. The other way round automates the error.
Buy in time, without buying too much

en.blog.el-pago-de-vacaciones-es-un-adelant: Holiday pay is an advance
Holidays
It's paid before the leave is taken and deducted afterwards. When that second step is missing, the company pays for the same day twice and never notices.
A mistake that produces no error
This is probably the most expensive payroll fault we've seen, and the quietest. It raises no alert, it throws no account visibly out, and nobody complains: the employee was overpaid.

The mechanism is simple. In the Dominican Republic, holiday pay is handed over before the employee leaves, so they have the money during the break. That means at that moment the company is paying for days that haven't happened yet.
When the period in which the employee is actually on leave arrives, their payslip is calculated as usual… and includes those days again. If nobody deducts them, they're paid twice.
The symptom isn't a mismatch: it's a staff cost slightly higher than it should be, spread across the year. Nobody looks for it because nobody knows it's there.
How the cycle really works
The full cycle has three moments, and the second is the one that gets forgotten:
The entitlement builds up. The employee accrues days according to their length of service. This is a balance, not a payment.
The advance is paid. Before leaving, they're handed the amount for the days they're about to take. In accounting terms it isn't an expense yet: it's a prepayment.
It's deducted when the leave is taken. On the payslip for the period they were away, those days are deducted because they were already paid. This is where the advance becomes an expense.

Skipping the third step is what produces the double payment. And it's easy to skip, because the second step is usually done by HR and the third by payroll, which is another process and sometimes another person.
The two balances that aren't the same
There's a distinction that confuses almost everyone, and it's worth being clear about because it decides different numbers:
Available days are the ones the employee can take right now. That's what you look at when approving a leave request.
Outstanding days are the ones you'd have to pay if they were settled today. That's what you look at when calculating a termination or a provision.

They don't match. An employee can have outstanding days that aren't available yet because they haven't reached the length of service that releases them. Using one balance where the other belonged gives a plausible, wrong figure — and plausible is the dangerous part, because nobody questions it.
The provision almost nobody keeps
There's a third effect, an accounting one this time. The holiday days employees have accrued and not taken are a debt of the company: if they all left tomorrow, you'd have to pay them.

When that provision isn't kept, the month's result looks better than it is, and the blow lands all at once in the month when several people leave or settle up. It's the same problem as with severance and notice pay, only with smaller figures and therefore less visible.
What to check in your payroll
If you're not sure whether this is happening to you, there are three quick checks:
Take an employee who went on leave a few months ago. Look at the payslip for the period they were away: is the deduction for the advanced days there? If it isn't, it was paid twice.
Compare the available days with the outstanding days of a long-serving employee. If the system gives you the same number for both, it's only keeping one.
Look for the holiday provision on the balance sheet. If it isn't there, the real liability is larger than the one shown.
This article describes the usual practice in the Dominican Republic. Accrual, seniority and settlement rules vary by country; confirm with your employment adviser before changing anything.

en.blog.tss-republica-dominicana-que-se-des: The TSS: what's deducted, what the employer contributes and where everyone gets it wrong
Social security
TSS errors are hardly ever about the rate: they're about the salary it's applied to. What counts towards the contribution base and why the cap changes the calculation.
They're two costs, not one

The first confusion is conceptual, and plenty of people who've run payroll for years have it: Dominican social security is paid by both sides. One part is deducted from the employee's salary; the other is contributed by the company on top of that salary.

That means an employee's real cost isn't their salary. It's their salary plus the employer contribution, and the difference isn't small. Budgeting a hire on the gross salary falls short systematically.
There are three schemes: family health insurance, pensions and occupational risks. On top comes the technical training levy, which is employer-only.
The real error: the base, not the rate
The rates are published and almost nobody gets them wrong. Where almost everybody does get it wrong is what they're applied to:
Not everything paid to an employee counts. Some items form part of the contributory salary and others don't. Putting an item in the wrong group skews the contribution every month.
There are caps. Above a certain salary, the contribution stops rising. A system that doesn't apply the cap overcharges the employee and overpays for the company, month after month.
The caps aren't the same for the three schemes. Applying one to all is an error that gives nearly-right figures, which is the worst kind of error.
An employee joining or leaving mid-month contributes for those days, not for the whole month.

A miscalculated contribution doesn't bounce: the TSS accepts it. The problem shows up when the employee goes to use their insurance or claim their pension and the weeks don't add up, and then the correction is retroactive.
Change reporting is half the work

What really eats the time each month isn't calculating: it's reporting changes. Joiners, leavers, salary changes, leave, benefits. If that's done by hand on the portal, it's done twice: once in the payroll system and once at the TSS.

And when it's done twice, sooner or later one of the two gets forgotten. The classic symptom: an employee who left three months ago and is still being paid contributions for, or one who joined and doesn't appear.
What the system should do
Classify every pay item as contributory or not, once, when it's defined, and not on every payslip.
Apply the cap that belongs to each scheme, with the current year's values.
Pro-rate mid-month joiners and leavers without anyone counting days by hand.
Generate the change file from the same data used to pay, not from a separate entry.
If you also handle severance, it's worth reading how severance and notice pay are calculated: they share the same salary base and the same classification errors.

Rates, caps and contributory items are updated by resolution, usually every year. Confirm the current ones with the TSS or your employment adviser: what's explained here is the mechanism, not the figures.
The TSS, calculated and filed from one place

en.blog.prestaciones-laborales-rd-cesantia-: Severance and notice pay: the debt that grows every month and isn't on the balance sheet
Severance benefits
Severance isn't generated when you dismiss: it's generated every month the employee stays. With no provision, an ordinary departure turns into a cash problem.
The debt that grows unseen
There's a very widespread wrong idea: that severance is an expense of the month someone leaves. It isn't. It builds up every month the employee stays at the company, even if nobody records it.

The consequence is a real debt that grows by itself and which, if not provisioned, doesn't appear in any financial statement until someone resigns. That month the result sinks, and not because the business went badly: because it had been reporting a better result than it had for months.

This is the calculation that springs the most surprises in a company with long-serving staff. Ten people with five, eight and twelve years aren't a minor contingency: they're several months of payroll waiting to be claimed.
What makes up the settlement
A departure settlement in the Dominican Republic combines several components, each with its own rule:
Notice. It depends on length of service and on who ends the contract. You can serve the notice or pay it.
Severance. It scales with length of service, and the scale isn't linear: the bands change the number of days per year.
Untaken holiday. This is where distinguishing outstanding days from available days matters, as we explain in the article on holiday pay.
The pro-rata share of the Christmas bonus for the time worked in the year.
The profit share or bonus, where applicable.

And above all: the reason for leaving changes what's paid. A dismissal without cause, a resignation and a termination for cause don't settle the same. A system that always calculates the same way is wrong in two of the three cases.
The salary used isn't last month's

Another point where it often goes wrong: the calculation base isn't «the salary». It's built from an average over a period and from the items that form part of ordinary pay, which aren't all the ones on the payslip.

Commissions, overtime and certain bonuses may or may not count, depending on their nature and regularity. Classifying them wrongly changes the whole settlement, and it's an error only discovered when the employee makes a claim.
Provisioning isn't optional (even if nobody makes you)

The way to stop this being a shock is to calculate each month what you'd owe if everyone left, and carry it as a provision. That turns a one-off blow into a spread expense, which is what it really is.
And it has a second effect you appreciate when the moment comes: knowing what a restructuring costs before deciding on it. Without the provision, that figure gets worked out by hand and late.
The provision is recalculated every month, with length of service updated.
It's broken down by component, because not all of them are paid in every case.
You can simulate a specific departure without having to carry it out.
The scales, the service bands and the items that go into the base are in the Labour Code and their interpretation can vary. Confirm each case with your employment adviser before settling.
Know what you owe before they ask for it
