en.blog.nomina-colombia-seguridad-social.ti: Payroll in Colombia: why the real cost is far more than the salary
en.blog.nomina-colombia-seguridad-social.re: Social security, payroll levies and statutory benefits. What's paid on top of the salary, what to provision, and why an all-inclusive salary isn't always the right call.
en.blog.nomina-colombia-seguridad-social.se: An employee's cost has three layers
Colombia is probably the country in the region where salary and real cost diverge most. Anyone budgeting on the wage falls short systematically, because there are three distinct layers on top:

Social security. Health, pension and occupational risk. Part is deducted from the employee's pay and part is contributed by the company. Occupational risk depends on the activity: it isn't the same for an office as for a building site.
Payroll levies. Contributions to training, family welfare and the compensation fund. They fall entirely on the company and there are exemptions depending on the salary level.
Statutory benefits. The service bonus, severance savings with their interest, and holidays. They aren't paid with the monthly payroll: they accrue and are paid on specific dates.
Statutory benefits are why a Colombian company can have a balanced year and still run out of cash in June and December: those months concentrate payments that built up all year.
Severance savings: the mechanism most misunderstood

Severance savings aren't paid to the employee monthly and don't stay with the company. They accrue through the year and are deposited into a fund on the due date. They also earn annual interest for the employee, which is paid directly.
The errors we see:
Not provisioning month by month, and discovering the full amount right before the deposit date.
Calculating the interest on the wrong balance, or over the wrong period.
Not allowing for authorised partial withdrawals, which change the balance.
Forgetting that an employee who joined mid-year has a pro-rata base, not a full one.
The transport allowance and each item's base

A small detail that throws many payrolls out: the transport allowance is paid below a certain salary level, and it counts towards the base of some things and not others. Putting it where it doesn't belong, or leaving it out where it does, changes benefits and contributions at once.

The general principle applies everywhere: every pay item has to be classified once — whether it contributes, whether it's a benefits base, whether it's salary or not — and the calculation inherits it. Classifying it on every payslip guarantees that one month it'll be done differently.
An all-inclusive salary isn't automatically better

Above a certain salary level you can agree an all-inclusive salary, which folds the statutory benefits into the salary itself. It simplifies payroll a lot, which is why it's often proposed as a solution.

But it isn't always the right call, and the decision isn't a payroll one: it's about cost and negotiation. What is certain is that it has a legal minimum and rules of its own, and applying it wrongly leaves the company exposed.

On top comes electronic payroll, which has to be transmitted on its own schedule. It feeds off the calculation: if the calculation is misclassified, so is the filing. We cover it alongside e-invoicing and the DIAN.
Rates, caps, exemption thresholds and the all-inclusive salary minimum are updated every year. Confirm the current figures with your employment adviser: what's explained here is the mechanism.

en.blog.nomina-costa-rica-ccss-aguinaldo.ti: Payroll in Costa Rica: the CCSS, the Christmas bonus and the provision that saves December
en.blog.nomina-costa-rica-ccss-aguinaldo.re: The Christmas bonus isn't a December expense: it's a whole-year expense paid in December. And Costa Rican social charges are among the highest in the region.
en.blog.nomina-costa-rica-ccss-aguinaldo.se: Social charges weigh, and it's worth knowing before you hire

Costa Rica has one of the highest social charge burdens in Central America, split between what's deducted from the employee and what the company contributes. Anyone arriving from another country in the region and budgeting with those figures gets a double-digit surprise.

The contribution covers sickness and maternity insurance, the disability, old-age and death scheme, and several additional funds. On top comes the workplace risk policy, which is compulsory and goes separately.
The payroll return is filed and paid on a fixed schedule. An unreported employee isn't a saving: it's a liability that surfaces at the first inspection, with the back periods recalculated.
The Christmas bonus: the thirteenth month you have to set aside
The Christmas bonus is an extra month's pay given in December, calculated on earnings over the relevant period. And here's the most repeated cash problem:

It builds up all year and is paid in one go. A company that doesn't provision month by month reaches December with a whole extra month of payroll that wasn't in the budget, right when there's also the year-end close and holidays.
The solution is accounting and it's simple: set aside a twelfth each month. The hard part isn't the calculation, it's remembering — which is why the system should do it, not a spreadsheet.
It's calculated on the average earned over the relevant period, not on December's salary.
The items that form part of salary count, and that's where the mistakes happen: commissions, overtime, regular bonuses.
An employee who joined mid-period gets the pro-rata share.
Holidays and settlement
Holiday accrues with time worked and, as across the region, accrued and untaken days are a debt of the company that's worth provisioning.

The settlement also includes notice and severance, with their own scales by length of service and reason for leaving. The underlying mechanism is the same one we describe for Dominican severance, though the scales and caps differ.
What the system should solve

Provision the Christmas bonus and holidays every month, without anyone having to remember.
Generate the payroll return from the same calculation used to pay.

en.blog.nomina-guatemala-igss-bono14-aguina: Payroll in Guatemala: two extra payments a year and a bonus that doesn't count
Payroll
Bono 14 in July, the Christmas bonus in December and an incentive allowance that stays out of the base. Three quirks that throw off any payroll imported from another country.
Two extra payments, at two points in the year
Guatemala has a quirk that surprises outsiders: there are two additional annual payments, not one. Bono 14 mid-year and the Christmas bonus at year end.

For the company's cash that means two peaks, not one. And for accounting, that you have to provision two things at once all year. A company that only provisions the Christmas bonus reaches July with half the problem solved.

Each has its own computation period, and they don't match the calendar year. Calculating both over the same period is one of the commonest errors when setting up Guatemalan payroll in a system designed for another country.
The incentive allowance: the item that breaks the calculations
There's an incentive allowance paid alongside the salary which is treated differently from ordinary pay: it doesn't form part of the base for certain calculations.
That detail, which looks minor, is what makes a payroll configured «like the country next door» give wrong figures systematically:
If it's put into the base of everything, you contribute too much and provision too much.
If it's left out of everything, you underpay where it should have counted.
And because the difference is small per employee, the total looks reasonable and nobody checks it.
It's the clearest argument for classifying every item once, when it's defined, instead of deciding it on every calculation.
The IGSS and the payroll return

Guatemalan social security is contributed by both employee and company, at different rates, and reported on a return with its own schedule. The usual errors are the usual ones: joiners and leavers reported late, and items wrongly classified as contributory.
The practical recommendation is the usual one: have the return come out of the same calculation used to pay. The moment there's a separate entry, differences appear.
Severance at termination

When the employment relationship ends, severance and the pro-rata shares of the annual payments and holidays come into play. The reason for termination changes what's due, so a system that always settles the same way is right only in some cases.
And as across the region, that severance builds up every month. Not provisioning it means reporting a better result than the real one until someone leaves.
IGSS rates, the incentive allowance amount and the computation periods are set by law and may be updated. Confirm what's current with the IGSS, the Ministry of Labour or your employment adviser.

en.blog.nomina-venezuela-salario-que-cambia: Payroll in Venezuela: when last month's salary no longer means the same
Payroll
The problem with Venezuelan payroll isn't the calculation: it's that the unit of measure moves. What to store, at what rate, and why history can't be reconverted.
The problem isn't calculating: it's what you measure with
A normal payroll is calculated once and stays. In Venezuela there's an added factor that changes everything: between calculating and paying, the value of the figure may have changed.

That turns decisions which elsewhere are administrative — what currency the salary is expressed in, at what rate it converts, when it's fixed — into business decisions taken continuously. And if the system doesn't record them properly, the history stops being comparable with itself.

The most damaging error is storing only the amount and converting it on display. That rewrites the past: the payslip from six months ago changes figure every time it's opened, and stops matching what the employee was paid.
What to store, and why
The rule that avoids almost every problem is the same as in invoicing: the amount and its rate travel together, and are never recalculated.
Every payslip stores the amount, the currency and the rate of its date. That's what the employee was paid, and it can't change afterwards.
Year-to-date totals are calculated by adding what was actually paid, not by reconverting history.
Accruing benefits are recorded using whatever criterion was agreed, and that criterion stays written down.
Reports can be viewed in any currency, but showing where each conversion came from.
The payslip's structure matters more than elsewhere

When a significant part of what the employee receives comes through items other than base salary, classifying each one stops being a detail: it decides what counts towards the benefits base and what doesn't.

And since those items tend to be the ones adjusted most often, a misclassified item is wrong at every revision. As in every other country, the fix is to classify once when the item is defined, not on every payslip.
What a system can actually solve
There are things a system doesn't fix — no tool stabilises an economy — but plenty that it does:
That each month's payslip can be reproduced exactly as issued, forever.
That staff cost can be seen in both currencies without redoing calculations.
That a general adjustment applies without touching each employee one by one.
That accrued benefits are calculated in the system, not on a separate spreadsheet.

The Venezuelan labour framework and its calculation criteria have particularities and have changed often. Confirm how they apply to your case with your employment adviser: what's explained here is how to handle the unit-of-measure problem, not the regulations.
Payroll in Venezuela?
Zyntello is multi-currency end to end: every payslip stores its rate, history isn't reconverted and reports come out in both currencies.
The wrong public holiday calendar gives away days and nobody notices
Payroll calculation
If the system uses a calendar that isn't the company's country's, holidays come out longer and overtime is paid wrongly. And the error gives no warning.
A defect you can only see by counting days

This is a real, measured error, and one of the best illustrations of why payroll is hard: a company using another country's holiday calendar hands out extra holiday days, and nothing in the system says so.

The mechanism is simple. When counting the days of a leave or a holiday, public holidays don't count as days taken. If the calendar has holidays that don't exist in that country, every request crossing them gives days back to the employee. Nobody complains: the employee comes out ahead and the system flags nothing.
The reverse is just as bad and does generate complaints: a missing holiday makes the employee spend a day of leave on a date when nobody was working.
Where it hits, beyond holidays
The calendar doesn't just decide holidays. It feeds several calculations at once:
Overtime and premiums. Working a public holiday is paid differently. If the date isn't flagged, it's paid as an ordinary day.
Working days for deadlines. A deadline falling «in three working days» depends on which days those are.
Shifts and planning. Covering a public holiday doesn't cost the same as covering a Tuesday.
Attendance. An absence on a non-working day isn't an absence.
The rule: the company's country decides the calendar

The operational conclusion is short: the calendar has to come from the company's country, and from a single source. Not from a list someone copied, not from a per-user setting, and certainly not from the server's locale.
And if the company operates in several countries, each of its entities uses its own. Sharing a calendar between countries is exactly how you give away days without realising.
The country's national holidays, updated every year.
The ones moved to a Monday, which don't always fall on their own date.
Local or regional ones, where they apply to a specific site.
A single place that answers «is this a working day?», used by every calculation.
It's the same principle as with holiday pay: what's calculated in two different places ends up giving two different numbers.
The right calendar, by country
In Zyntello the company's country decides its holiday calendar, and every calculation — holidays, premiums, deadlines — asks the same place.

en.blog.restaurante-cuadre-de-turno.titulo: Restaurants: why the shift never balances and how to fix it
en.blog.restaurante-cuadre-de-turno.resumen: A restaurant till goes out for specific reasons: comps, cancellations after the ticket prints, tips and staff meals.
en.blog.restaurante-cuadre-de-turno.seccion: The tensest moment of the day
Closing a shift in a restaurant pairs the most tired person of the day with the task that allows the least error. And it almost always comes out short.
The interesting part is that the causes are few and repeat, so they can be closed one by one.
Comps and courtesies. The dessert on the house, the round from the manager. If they aren't recorded as comps, they show up as missing stock.
Cancellations after the order goes to the kitchen. The dish was made and thrown away. The product left inventory and there's no sale behind it.
Tips. They come in with the payment and they aren't the business's revenue. Mixed into sales, the till runs over and the sales report lies.
Staff meals. The shift meal comes out of the same inventory. Unrecorded, it's shrinkage with no explanation.
Table changes and split bills. Where most lines go missing: a bill split three ways and one of the parts never gets charged.
Voids with no reason. If you can void without saying why and without a name attached, the shortfall has no owner.

Comps and post-order cancellations are the two most underrated, and they're the ones that connect the till to inventory. A restaurant that doesn't record them can't know its food cost, however well the cash balances.
Every shift with its opening, its owner and its float. The shortfall has a name; it isn't «the till's».
Comps, cancellations and staff meals each with their own record type and reason.
Tips separated from revenue at the point of payment.
Voids with a mandatory reason and the name of who did it.
The count compares what was counted with what was expected and records the result, with no way to force it to balance.
And what ties it all together: every dish sold deducts its ingredients. Without that, a restaurant's inventory is an inventory of purchases, not of consumption.
Zyntello's Restaurant module runs the shift with its owner, comps and cancellations with a reason, and deducts each dish's recipe.
en.blog.condominios-cobrar-la-cuota-a-tiemp: Condominiums: why the fee doesn't get collected and the fund never stretches
Condominiums
Arrears in a condominium aren't a collections problem: they're a transparency problem. Whoever can't see where the money goes stops paying.
The circle that feeds itself

Running a condominium has a problem that feeds itself: whoever doesn't understand what their fee is spent on stops paying it. And the fewer who pay, the worse the building is kept, which gives more reasons not to pay.
Breaking that circle is less about chasing and more about every owner seeing, without having to ask, what they owe and where what they paid went.
What fails in practice
The statement arrives late or not at all. The owner finds out they owe when they already owe three months.
Late fees get applied by eye. Sometimes yes, sometimes no, depending on who complains. The moment it's known to be negotiable, it stops deterring.
Payments can't be identified. Transfers with no reference and nobody knows which apartment they're from.
Special levies get mixed with regular fees, and the owner can't tell what's maintenance and what's the lift levy.
Nobody sees where it's spent. The report is presented at the general meeting, once a year, on paper.
What changes when it's solved
A statement available at any time, not when someone asks for it. What people can see, they pay.
Late fees calculated by rule, the same for everyone and automatic. It stops being a negotiation.
An automatic receipt when payment comes in, with the reference that identifies the unit.
Regular and special levies kept apart, each with its purpose.
Spending in plain sight: where the money went, by line and by month.
A reserve fund with its balance, so a special levy isn't always the only way out.

The most effective measure is usually the simplest: let every owner see their balance and the common spending whenever they want. Arrears fall without anyone chasing anyone, because the suspicion that money is going missing disappears.
Fees that collect themselves
Zyntello Condominiums runs the fees, rule-based late charges, the owner portal and the reserve fund with its balance in plain sight.

en.blog.prestamos-mora-e-intereses-como-se-: Loans and credit sales: where late-interest calculations go wrong
Finance
Interest calculated wrongly doesn't throw an error: it gives a plausible number. And across a loan book, a small error repeated a thousand times is a lot of money.
The worst error is the one that looks right
In a loan book, calculation errors don't produce error messages: they produce instalments slightly different from what they should be. And because they look reasonable, nobody checks them.
Multiplied by hundreds of customers and dozens of instalments, a small systematic error is a lot of money — and, depending on the case, a problem with the customer or with the regulator.
Where the calculations go wrong
The day-count basis. Calculating on 360 or on 365 days gives different results. Neither is wrong; mixing them is.

Which balance late interest runs on. On the overdue instalment, on that instalment's principal, on the whole loan? They're three very different figures, and you have to pick one, write it down and stick to it.
The order payments are applied in. A payment that doesn't cover everything — what does it go to first: late interest, interest or principal? The order changes the final balance and the term.
Grace days. If they exist, does late interest run from the due date or from the end of grace? Both get implemented, and they give different numbers.
Rounding. Rounding each instalment or rounding at the end changes the total. It's cents per instalment, and thousands across the book.

The check that reveals it: take a real loan, work out the schedule by hand in a spreadsheet and compare it with the system's, instalment by instalment. If there's a difference at instalment 18, there'll be one in every loan.
The cases that break systems
Anyone can do the normal calculation. What sets a serious lending system apart is how it handles what isn't normal:
The extra payment to principal. Does it cut the instalment or the term? The customer should be able to choose, and the schedule gets rebuilt.
Refinancing. A loan that's restructured isn't a new one: the history has to be kept.
The repeated part payment. Someone who always pays a bit less creates a carry-forward that has to be tracked precisely.
Waivers. Forgiving late interest is a decision with a name and a reason, not an adjustment.
And what you need to see of the book

Beyond the individual calculation, the management question is how much of what you lent you'll get back. That means seeing the book by arrears buckets, its trend, and how much sits with a few customers — the same reasoning as in ageing reports, with higher stakes.
Lending is regulated differently in every country, with limits and requirements to meet. Confirm your framework with an adviser before setting rates and charges.
Calculations that survive an audit

en.blog.servicios-recurrentes-lo-que-se-esc: Service businesses: what slips away between the job and the payment
Services
In a car wash, a workshop or a clinic the product is time, and time leaves no trace if nobody records it. Where the money goes.
When the product can't be counted
In a service business there's no shelf to count. If a wash, a repair or an appointment wasn't recorded, there's no way to find out later: no stock is missing.
That means the same slips a shop would catch at stocktake stay here forever.
Where the money slips away
The service delivered and never charged. The customer was seen, the work was done and nobody raised the bill. At a busy counter, it happens more than you'd think.
The extra that never made the bill. A treatment, a part or a test was added, and it stayed off the bill.
The discount given verbally, different depending on who's serving and with no record of who authorised it.
The supply used that never gets deducted. The cleaning product, the workshop material. The service was charged, but the cost never went in.
The no-show. It isn't just the lost revenue: it's the slot that could have gone to someone else.
The technician's commission calculated from a sheet that doesn't match what was invoiced.
The most expensive is the fourth and hardly anyone looks at it: if the supply isn't deducted, the service looks more profitable than it is. Prices keep being quoted on a cost that doesn't exist.
What closes it
Open the job when it starts, not when it's paid. An open job is a visible outstanding bill; a service with no job doesn't exist.
Add extras to the job as they happen, not from memory at the end.
Cap the discount and record who gave it.
Give every service its defined consumption and deduct it on completion.
Make the diary and the billing the same thing, so an appointment that was seen can't end up without a bill.
And what turns this into recurring business: knowing when they're due back. The six-month service, the yearly check-up. A customer who returns because you reminded them costs far less than a new one.
No service slips through
Zyntello has modules for car washes, workshops and clinics: the job opens when work starts, extras are added as they happen and supplies deduct themselves.

en.nos.p1: Zyntello, S.R.L. develops, deploys and sells enterprise technology solutions based on Artificial Intelligence, process automation and specialised information technology consulting.
en.nos.p2: We support companies, SMEs and public sector bodies through their digital transformation, with more than two decades of experience in IT infrastructure, ERP systems, software development and automation.

en.pri.automatizacion.resumen: What a company really automates —approvals, reconciliation, collections, reports— and where to start so it shows within weeks.
en.pri.automatizacion.heroTitulo: Half of office work is moving data from one place to another
en.pri.automatizacion.heroBajada: Approving a purchase over WhatsApp, keying in the supplier's invoice, matching the bank line by line, building the same report every Monday. None of that is the business: it's the toll for not having automated it. This explains what can be taken out of the way, and in what order.
en.pri.automatizacion.problema.titulo: Manual work shows up in no income statement
en.pri.automatizacion.problema.texto: Nobody invoices «three hours matching the bank». That's why the cost of repetitive work is invisible: it shows in no report, it has no owner, and it's never the urgent thing. It shows up elsewhere —in closings that run late, in the collection that was forgotten, in the person who can't take holidays because only they know how that process works.
en.pri.automatizacion.problema.puntos.0: The same piece of data is keyed into three different systems
en.pri.automatizacion.problema.puntos.1: An approval is asked for over WhatsApp and recorded nowhere
en.pri.automatizacion.problema.puntos.2: Month-end close depends on one specific person being available
en.pri.automatizacion.problema.puntos.3: Overdue receivables are discovered once the customer no longer answers
en.pri.automatizacion.problema.puntos.4: Every report is built by hand and never twice the same
en.pri.automatizacion.problema.puntos.5: When someone leaves, their process leaves with them
en.pri.automatizacion.beneficios.0.descripc: Who approved, when, and for how much is written down. No more «I told you in a message»: if it isn't approved, the document doesn't move.
en.pri.automatizacion.beneficios.1.descripc: The supplier's invoice comes in as data, not as a PDF for someone to key in. What doesn't add up is flagged for review instead of slipping through.
en.pri.automatizacion.beneficios.2.descripc: The system proposes the match between the bank movement and the document, and a person confirms it. What changes isn't the accuracy: it's the time.
en.pri.automatizacion.beneficios.3.descripc: The receivable about to fall due, the stock about to run out, the contract about to expire. A timely alert is worth more than the best report of what already happened.
en.pri.automatizacion.beneficios.4.descripc: The same report, on the same day, from the system's data and not from a spreadsheet somebody keeps on the side. And if nobody opens it, that's known too.
en.pri.automatizacion.beneficios.5.titulo: AI agents where judgement is needed
en.pri.automatizacion.beneficios.5.descripc: Classifying an expense, drafting a reply to a customer, summarising what happened this week. Where judgement is needed and a fixed rule won't do.
en.pri.automatizacion.detalles.0.titulo: Automating a broken process breaks it faster
en.pri.automatizacion.detalles.0.descripcio: If the way purchases get approved today isn't clear, automating it multiplies the mess. First you define who decides what; then you automate. That order isn't optional.
en.pri.automatizacion.detalles.1.titulo: The exception is where everything falls apart
en.pri.automatizacion.detalles.1.descripcio: 80% of cases are easy. The value lies in what the system does with the 20% that doesn't fit: if it blocks them silently, someone will end up going around it, and you're back where you started.
en.pri.automatizacion.detalles.2.titulo: An alert that always arrives stops being read
en.pri.automatizacion.detalles.2.descripcio: An alert that fires every day becomes noise in two weeks. You tune the threshold until firing means something, or the alert is worth nothing.
en.pri.automatizacion.detalles.3.descripcio: An automated process that leaves no trace of what it did and why is impossible to audit and to correct. Every step is logged, including the one an AI decided.
en.pri.automatizacion.detalles.4.descripcio: Approving a payment, writing off a debt, letting someone go. Automation prepares the decision and carries it out; it doesn't make it.
en.pri.automatizacion.detalles.5.titulo: You start with the boring, not the flashy
en.pri.automatizacion.detalles.5.descripcio: The first process to automate is the most repetitive and the least arguable. The eye-catching part —the agent that talks to customers— comes later, once the data underneath is reliable.
en.pri.automatizacion.cifras.2.etiqueta: countries, each with its own rules
en.pri.automatizacion.pasos.0.titulo: Look at what is done today
en.pri.automatizacion.pasos.0.descripcion: Not what the manual says: what people actually do, with their spreadsheets and their messages. That's where the real process lives.
en.pri.automatizacion.pasos.1.titulo: Pick one and do it end to end
en.pri.automatizacion.pasos.1.descripcion: One complete process in production is worth more than six half-done. The first one is what proves whether this works, so you pick it by pain, not by ease.
en.pri.automatizacion.pasos.2.titulo: Measure, then move to the next
en.pri.automatizacion.pasos.2.descripcion: How long it took before and how long now. If it can't be measured, you don't know whether it worked, and the second process gets chosen blind.
en.pri.automatizacion.publico.0.titulo: The company that already has a system
en.pri.automatizacion.publico.0.descripcion: You have an ERP or several programs, but between them there are people moving data by hand. That's where it shows fastest.
en.pri.automatizacion.publico.1.titulo: The one growing faster than its team
en.pri.automatizacion.publico.1.descripcion: Volume is going up and the answer so far has been to hire. Automating first tells you how many people you actually need.
en.pri.automatizacion.publico.2.titulo: The one that depends on one person
en.pri.automatizacion.publico.2.descripcion: There's a process only one specific person knows how to run. That isn't a productivity problem: it's a risk.
en.pri.automatizacion.faq.0.pregunta: Do we have to change systems to automate?
en.pri.automatizacion.faq.0.respuesta: Not necessarily. Part of what gets automated are the links between what you already have. That said, if the source data sits in three places and none of them agree, the first step isn't to automate: it's to decide which one is authoritative.
en.pri.automatizacion.faq.1.respuesta: A specific process —an approval, a collection reminder, a recurring report— goes live in weeks. What takes months is automating an entire company, and that's why nobody starts there.
en.pri.automatizacion.faq.2.respuesta: In our experience, what it replaces are the hours nobody wanted to do. People are still there, deciding and serving customers, instead of typing in what a PDF already says.
en.pri.automatizacion.faq.3.pregunta: What if the AI gets it wrong?
en.pri.automatizacion.faq.3.respuesta: That's why whatever an AI decides is logged, and whatever isn't clear is flagged for human review instead of being executed. An automation that can't be seen to make a mistake is an automation you can't trust.
en.pri.automatizacion.faq.4.pregunta: Is it worth it for a small company?
en.pri.automatizacion.faq.4.respuesta: Yes, and sometimes more so: in a small company the manual process eats the owner's time, which is exactly the most expensive time there is. You start with one module and grow from there.
en.pri.automatizacion.faq.5.pregunta: Can the tax side be automated?
en.pri.automatizacion.faq.5.respuesta: Yes. Tax documents, withholdings and the filings for each country's authority are inside the platform —NCF in the Dominican Republic, and the equivalent in Venezuela, Colombia, Guatemala and Costa Rica.

en.pri.nosotros.resumen: Zyntello, S.R.L. is a Dominican technology company with more than 20 years implementing management systems. We develop our own platform.
en.pri.nosotros.heroTitulo: Twenty years implementing systems before writing our own
en.pri.nosotros.heroBajada: Zyntello, S.R.L. did not start as a product. It started implementing other people's systems —Softland, Profit, infrastructure, cloud— and seeing up close why so many ERP projects end up abandoned. The platform we sell today is the consequence of that.
en.pri.nosotros.problema.titulo: Hardly anyone abandons an ERP because a feature is missing
en.pri.nosotros.problema.texto: They abandon it because nobody explained what that screen was for, because the project took so long that the business had already changed, or because when something broke there was nobody to call. The software is hardly ever the hard part. The hard part is everything around it, and that's only learned by having done it many times.
en.pri.nosotros.problema.puntos.0: Implementation projects that outlast the company's patience
en.pri.nosotros.problema.puntos.1: Systems nobody was taught to use, filled in wrong from day one
en.pri.nosotros.problema.puntos.2: A vendor who disappears once the install is done
en.pri.nosotros.problema.puntos.3: Programs that don't talk to each other and force double keying
en.pri.nosotros.problema.puntos.4: Solutions designed for another country and its tax rules
en.pri.nosotros.problema.puntos.5: Big vendors who don't return a small customer's call
en.pri.nosotros.beneficios.0.titulo: We're the ones who build it
en.pri.nosotros.beneficios.0.descripcion: The platform is ours. When something needs changing, there's no ticket to raise with a vendor on another continent and no waiting for the next release.
en.pri.nosotros.beneficios.1.titulo: We know the region's tax rules
en.pri.nosotros.beneficios.1.descripcion: Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Colombia, Guatemala and Costa Rica. Each with its own tax document, its withholdings and its filings to the relevant authority.
en.pri.nosotros.beneficios.2.titulo: We come from implementing, not from selling
en.pri.nosotros.beneficios.2.descripcion: More than a hundred projects delivered before having a product of our own. That decides design choices you don't see in a demo but feel six months in.
en.pri.nosotros.beneficios.3.descripcion: Support has a published Service Level Agreement and a channel of its own. The moment a vendor disappears is exactly when they start being needed.
en.pri.nosotros.beneficios.4.titulo: We work with companies of any size
en.pri.nosotros.beneficios.4.descripcion: The same system serves a hardware store and a group with several companies. What changes is which modules get switched on.
en.pri.nosotros.beneficios.5.titulo: We also do what isn't our product
en.pri.nosotros.beneficios.5.descripcion: Infrastructure, cloud, cybersecurity, custom development and IT staffing. Sometimes the right answer to a problem isn't selling another module.
en.pri.nosotros.detalles.0.titulo: Help is written at the same time as the screen
en.pri.nosotros.detalles.0.descripcion: Every screen ships with its help, its field-by-field explanations and its data dictionary. A screen that isn't explained is a screen that gets filled in wrong.
en.pri.nosotros.detalles.1.titulo: One customer's data never touches another's
en.pri.nosotros.detalles.1.descripcion: Isolation between subscribers, and between the companies of a single subscriber, is the rule that ranks above every other technical consideration in the project.
en.pri.nosotros.detalles.2.descripcion: Modules don't sync with each other: they read the same data. That difference is what makes it impossible for inventory and accounting to disagree.
en.pri.nosotros.detalles.3.titulo: The product grows from what's learned in operation
en.pri.nosotros.detalles.3.descripcion: A good part of what the platform does today came out of a real problem from a real customer, not from a competitor's feature list.
en.pri.nosotros.detalles.4.titulo: We work remotely and on site
en.pri.nosotros.detalles.4.descripcion: The platform runs in the browser, but when a visit is needed, we go. There are customers in five countries and not every problem gets solved over a video call.
en.pri.nosotros.detalles.5.titulo: What we don't know how to do, we say so
en.pri.nosotros.detalles.5.descripcion: Some jobs don't fit what we're good at. Saying so beforehand costs a sale; not saying so costs a customer and their recommendation.

en.pri.nosotros.pasos.0.titulo: We listen to what's failing today
en.pri.nosotros.pasos.0.descripcion: Before proposing anything. Most of the time, the problem people describe isn't the one costing the most money.
en.pri.nosotros.pasos.1.titulo: We propose the minimum that solves it
en.pri.nosotros.pasos.1.descripcion: A module, not a project. If less fixes it, less it is.
en.pri.nosotros.pasos.2.descripcion: Go-live is the beginning. What decides whether the system is still used a year from now is what happens afterwards.
en.pri.nosotros.publico.0.titulo: If you're about to change systems
en.pri.nosotros.publico.0.descripcion: It's worth talking to someone who has implemented other people's and knows where projects usually break.
en.pri.nosotros.publico.1.titulo: If you already have one and it isn't working
en.pri.nosotros.publico.1.descripcion: Sometimes you don't have to change everything. You have to fix the specific piece that's failing.
en.pri.nosotros.publico.2.titulo: If you operate in several countries
en.pri.nosotros.publico.2.descripcion: Each country has its own tax rules and its own way of doing things. Having five in the same system saves you five systems.
en.pri.nosotros.faq.0.respuesta: Zyntello, S.R.L. is a Dominican company. We operate in the Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Colombia, Guatemala and Costa Rica, and we give remote support to customers outside those countries.
en.pri.nosotros.faq.1.pregunta: Is the platform yours, or do you resell a product?
en.pri.nosotros.faq.1.respuesta: It's ours. We build and maintain it, which is what lets a needed change actually be made instead of being requested from a vendor.
en.pri.nosotros.faq.2.pregunta: Do you only work with your own platform?
en.pri.nosotros.faq.2.respuesta: No. We also do infrastructure, cloud, cybersecurity, custom development, technical support and specialist IT staffing. They're in the services section.
en.pri.nosotros.faq.3.pregunta: What happens to my data if I stop being a customer?
en.pri.nosotros.faq.3.respuesta: They're yours and they're handed over to you. There's a published page with the data deletion procedure and a privacy policy explaining what is kept and why.
en.pri.nosotros.faq.4.pregunta: Do you work with small companies?
en.pri.nosotros.faq.4.respuesta: Yes. In fact the per-module model exists precisely for that: so a small company can start with one piece without buying an entire system.
en.pri.nosotros.faq.5.pregunta: How do I get in touch?
en.pri.nosotros.faq.5.respuesta: Over WhatsApp at +1 829 639 9877 or by writing to info@zyntello.com. If you're already a customer, the support channel is soporte@zyntello.com.
en.pri.precios.subtitulo: What it costs and what's included
en.pri.precios.resumen: Monthly subscription per module, with no upfront licence, no implementation project and no lock-in. You subscribe to what you use and add the rest later.
en.pri.precios.heroTitulo: You pay for the modules you use, and no others
en.pri.precios.heroBajada: There's no upfront licence, no implementation project to bill before you start, and no twenty-module bundle of which you'll use three. You subscribe monthly to what you need today and add the rest when the business asks for it.
en.pri.precios.segundoBoton.texto: See the modules and their prices
en.pri.precios.problema.titulo: The price of an ERP is almost never the price of an ERP
en.pri.precios.problema.texto: The number on the quote is the small part. Underneath there's usually an implementation billed separately, a minimum bundle you must take even if you won't use it, a multi-year lock-in and a per-user cost that grows every time someone joins. Add it all up and the real figure shows once the contract is signed.

en.pri.precios.publico.1.titulo: The one that has one and doesn't use it
en.pri.precios.publico.1.descripcion: You paid for a big licence and the company still works in Excel on the side. More training won't fix that.
en.pri.precios.publico.2.titulo: The one that only needs one piece
en.pri.precios.publico.2.descripcion: Your accounting works, but payroll or inventory doesn't. You don't have to change everything to fix one part.
en.pri.precios.faq.0.pregunta: Where can I see each module's price?
en.pri.precios.faq.0.respuesta: In the modules section of zyntello.com. Each module shows its monthly price and links to the page explaining what it does and who it's for.
en.pri.precios.faq.1.respuesta: The subscription is per module. If your case has an unusual number of users we'll talk it through, but the published price is not a per-head price.
en.pri.precios.faq.2.respuesta: Not to get going: modules come configured with your country's tax rules. What is quoted separately is migrating data from a previous system, custom development and on-site training.
en.pri.precios.faq.3.pregunta: What if I want to cancel?
en.pri.precios.faq.3.respuesta: There's no lock-in. You drop the module and the charge stops. Your data is yours and it's handed over to you; there's a data deletion page with the procedure.
en.pri.precios.faq.4.respuesta: No. Adapting to the rules of the countries we operate in is part of the subscription, like every other update.
en.pri.precios.faq.5.pregunta: Can I start with one module and add more later?
en.pri.precios.faq.5.respuesta: That's the recommended way. All 34 modules share the same database, so adding a new one isn't a migration: the data that's already there is already there.
en.pri.precios.faq.6.respuesta: It's agreed when you sign up. Signing up happens over WhatsApp or email; there's no card payment on the website.
en.pri.precios.faq.7.pregunta: Is there a discount for paying yearly?
en.pri.precios.faq.7.respuesta: It's discussed case by case. Write to us and we'll tell you what we can do with your combination of modules.
en.fun.aprobaciones.subtitulo: Who authorises what, written down once
en.fun.aprobaciones.resumen: A single approval engine across 16 modules. You define who approves what and from what amount, and the document does not move until someone signs it.
en.fun.aprobaciones.heroBajada: One approval engine for all 16 modules: purchasing, payments, invoices, payroll, inventory adjustments, journal entries, budget. You define once who authorises what and from what amount — and every signature leaves a record.
en.fun.aprobaciones.problema.titulo: When authorising means asking around, nobody knows who said yes
en.fun.aprobaciones.problema.texto: In most companies, authorisation lives in a WhatsApp message, an email or a corridor conversation. It works until the day someone has to explain who approved a two-hundred-thousand purchase, and then there is no document — only memories that do not match. And meanwhile, nobody can see what is waiting for approval.
en.fun.aprobaciones.problema.puntos.0: A large purchase is approved verbally and leaves no record
en.fun.aprobaciones.problema.puntos.1: Nobody knows what is waiting for their signature right now
en.fun.aprobaciones.problema.puntos.2: The approver goes away and everything stops
en.fun.aprobaciones.problema.puntos.3: Each module has its own way of authorising, or none at all
en.fun.aprobaciones.problema.puntos.4: You find out something was never approved once it is already done
en.fun.aprobaciones.problema.puntos.5: There is no way to prove who authorised what, or when
en.fun.aprobaciones.beneficios.0.descripcio: Purchasing, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Invoicing, Inventory, Payroll, Banks, Cash Register, Petty Cash, Accounting, Fixed Assets, Budget, CRM, ConstructFlow, Prestamello and Support all use the same one. The rule is defined once, not sixteen times.
en.fun.aprobaciones.beneficios.1.descripcio: Up to X the area manager approves it; above that, senior management. The line is written once and stops being argued over on every document.
en.fun.aprobaciones.beneficios.2.descripcio: It is not a warning you can ignore: the engine blocks execution. Anything awaiting approval is not paid, not shipped and not posted.
en.fun.aprobaciones.beneficios.3.titulo: An inbox of what is pending
en.fun.aprobaciones.beneficios.3.descripcio: Each approver sees their own items in a list, with how long each has been waiting. What has been stuck for three days is visible, instead of surfacing when someone complains.
en.fun.aprobaciones.beneficios.4.titulo: A full trail of every decision
en.fun.aprobaciones.beneficios.4.descripcio: Who requested it, who approved or rejected it, when, and with what note. It is what turns "I think Juan approved it" into a document.
en.fun.aprobaciones.beneficios.5.descripcio: It does not just sit as a status: it returns the document to where it belongs, so whoever requested it can fix it instead of starting over.
en.fun.aprobaciones.cifras.2.etiqueta: it does not warn: it prevents
en.fun.aprobaciones.detalles.0.titulo: Approving and executing are one act
en.fun.aprobaciones.detalles.0.descripcion: On approval the document applies itself: the order goes out, the payment joins the run, the entry is posted. Separating the two is what leaves things approved and undone.
en.fun.aprobaciones.detalles.1.titulo: A single approver is a single point of failure
en.fun.aprobaciones.detalles.1.descripcion: That is why every level takes more than one. With a single approver, their holiday stops the company's purchasing — and nobody saw it coming when setting it up.
en.fun.aprobaciones.detalles.2.descripcion: Rejecting without saying why forces a conversation to find out — and that conversation is exactly what the workflow was meant to avoid.
en.fun.aprobaciones.detalles.3.titulo: Each module brings its own meaning
en.fun.aprobaciones.detalles.3.descripcion: The engine is shared, but approving an invoice does not mean the same as approving an inventory adjustment. Each module defines its own effect without rewriting the workflow.
en.fun.aprobaciones.detalles.4.descripcion: If the document no longer applies, the request is withdrawn instead of sitting in someone's inbox forever.
en.fun.aprobaciones.detalles.5.descripcion: And the requester gets one when it is resolved. A workflow that depends on someone remembering to check the inbox is a workflow that stalls on Fridays.
en.fun.aprobaciones.pasos.0.descripcion: Who approves, from what amount, and how many approvers per band.
en.fun.aprobaciones.pasos.1.descripcion: By module and document type: not everything needs a signature.
en.fun.aprobaciones.pasos.2.descripcion: What is pending is visible, you approve or reject it, and the document carries on by itself.
en.fun.aprobaciones.publico.0.titulo: You have more than one level of decision
en.fun.aprobaciones.publico.0.descripcion: And today authorisation is requested by message.
en.fun.aprobaciones.publico.1.descripcion: And you have to prove who authorised each thing.
en.fun.aprobaciones.publico.2.descripcion: Because nobody knows what is waiting for their signature.
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.0.pregunta: Do I have to buy it separately?
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.0.respuesta: No. It comes with the platform and runs across every module you have subscribed to. It is not a paid add-on.
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.1.pregunta: Can I require approval only above a certain amount?
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.1.respuesta: Yes, that is the usual way: you define amount bands and each one has its own approvers.
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.2.pregunta: What happens if the approver is on holiday?
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.2.respuesta: That is why each level takes several approvers. With only one, their absence stops the process — and it is worth planning for that when setting it up.
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.3.pregunta: Can I approve from my phone?
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.3.respuesta: Yes: the inbox is just another screen of the platform and works in a mobile browser.
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.4.pregunta: Is there a record for an audit?
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.4.respuesta: Yes: who requested, who resolved, when and with what note, tied to the document that triggered the request.
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.5.pregunta: And if I approve something by mistake?
en.fun.aprobaciones.faq.5.respuesta: Approval executes the document, so you correct it the way that document allows — a credit note, a reversing entry — and that correction is recorded too.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.subtitulo: What every data field means, written down
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.resumen: 593 tables and 5,612 columns documented in plain language, with what each one means and what changes it. Your data stops being a secret kept by whoever programmed it.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.heroTitulo: Your data, explained one by one
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.heroBajada: 593 tables and 5,612 columns documented in plain language: what each one holds, which module writes it and what happens if it changes. It is what keeps your information yours even if you change supplier.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.problema.titulo: The data is yours — but only if you know what it means
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.problema.texto: Any ERP stores your data. Very few tell you what it means. When an audit arrives, or an integration, or simply a new hire, the question "what exactly is this column?" can only be answered by whoever built the system — and that ties you to them far more tightly than any contract.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.problema.puntos: Nobody knows exactly what a field means
Integrating another system means guessing the structure
An audit asks where a figure comes from and there is no answer
Only one person knows the database
Moving to another system means starting from scratch
Two departments use the same word for different things
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.beneficios.0.de: Not the technical names: what the data means in your business, in plain language and written for someone who did not build the system.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.beneficios.1.de: Each one with what it holds, which module writes it and what it relates to. The structure of your information stops being a map only one person has.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.beneficios.2.de: What is documented is what can be queried. The dictionary is not an appendix: it is what keeps building a report from being guesswork.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.beneficios.3.de: Where each figure comes from, field by field. Answering that with a document instead of an explanation shortens an entire audit.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.beneficios.4.de: When you need to connect another system, the structure is already written down. You do not have to infer it from sample data.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.beneficios.5.ti: It stays current with the product
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.beneficios.5.de: A new table without its documentation turns the test suite red. It is not a promise to keep it up to date: it is a ratchet.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.detalles.0.titu: It explains the DATA, not the column
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.detalles.0.desc: Saying that `monto_neto` is "the net amount" explains nothing. The entry says what it includes, what it leaves out and who calculates it.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.detalles.1.titu: It says which module WRITES each table
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.detalles.1.desc: It is the hardest question when something does not add up: knowing which module sets that value saves hunting through the whole system.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.detalles.2.titu: A column with two owners does not fail: it stays silent
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.detalles.2.desc: When two modules write the same field, the result looks right and is wrong. Documenting it is what makes it visible.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.detalles.3.titu: Removing a table from the dictionary has consequences
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.detalles.3.desc: What is documented feeds the report builder. Removing or adding a table changes what can be queried, which is why it is not a cosmetic change.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.detalles.4.desc: The catalogues Zyntello maintains — countries, currencies, the tax register, ports — are kept apart from your operational data, which is the data that is yours.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.detalles.5.titu: It is your insurance against lock-in
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.detalles.5.desc: A supplier who does not document your data ties you down without saying so. With the dictionary, changing systems is a project; without it, it is starting from scratch.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.pasos.0.descrip: It is inside the platform, with nothing to request and nothing extra to pay.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.pasos.1.titulo: Find the table or the field
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.pasos.1.descrip: By module, by name or by what it describes.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.pasos.2.descrip: For a report, for an integration or to answer an audit.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.publico.0.descr: And you have to explain where each figure comes from.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.publico.1.titul: You are about to integrate another system
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.publico.1.descr: And you need to know what is inside without guessing.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.publico.2.titul: You do not want to depend on one supplier
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.publico.2.descr: And your data must stay readable without them.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.faq.0.pregunta: Do I have to buy it separately?
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.faq.0.respuesta: No. It comes with the platform and covers the modules you have subscribed to.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.faq.1.respuesta: Yes, all of it — written in Spanish inside the platform. And it does not describe the technical column: it describes what that data means in your business.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.faq.2.pregunta: Is it useful for integrating with another system?
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.faq.2.respuesta: Yes: it is the structure written down, so connecting something stops requiring reverse engineering from sample data.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.faq.3.pregunta: Is it kept up to date?
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.faq.3.respuesta: Yes — and not out of goodwill: a new table without its documentation turns the test suite red.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.faq.4.pregunta: How does it relate to the reports?
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.faq.4.respuesta: What is documented is what the report builder can query. The dictionary is what keeps building a report from being guesswork.
en.fun.diccionario-de-datos.faq.5.respuesta: Yes, to take it into an audit or into the conversation with whoever is going to integrate with you.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.subtitulo: The report you are missing, without waiting for anyone
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.resumen: Build your own reports over your own data without writing a query, from curated sources always scoped to your company. Export to PDF, Excel, CSV and TXT.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.heroTitulo: The question no report answers, answered by you
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.heroBajada: You pick the source, the columns, the filters and the totals — and out comes the report. No SQL, no support ticket and no giving anyone access to the database.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.problema.titul: Every company has questions no standard report answers
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.problema.texto: An ERP ships hundreds of reports and yours is still missing: the specific cross-reference your business needs to look at every Monday. When you have to ask for it, the answer arrives weeks later or arrives wrong; meanwhile you decide with whatever you have, or export to Excel to redo the same cross-reference by hand every month.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.problema.punto: Your specific business question has no report
Asking for a new one takes weeks and costs money
You export to Excel and redo the same cross-reference every month
Nobody can reproduce where a figure came from
Granting database access to "get it out quickly" is a risk
Someone has to remember to send the Monday report
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.beneficios.0.d: You pick the source and then its columns, filters, sorting and totals. It is used by whoever knows the business, not whoever knows the database.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.beneficios.1.t: Header and lines, not just flat lists
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.beneficios.1.d: A document with its lines: invoices with their items, payments with the documents they settle. That is the shape of most real questions.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.beneficios.2.d: Each source exposes chosen fields, always scoped to your company. There is no way to ask for data that is not yours, nor to cross what must not be crossed.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.beneficios.3.d: PDF to present, Excel and CSV to keep working, TXT to load it into another system. Four formats from the same report.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.beneficios.4.d: Who ran what, when and with which filters. It is what lets you reproduce a figure someone questions three months later.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.beneficios.5.d: It builds itself and arrives at whatever interval you set. Remembering the Monday report stops being somebody's job.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.cifras.0.etiqu: built by whoever knows the business
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.cifras.1.etiqu: formats: PDF, Excel, CSV and TXT
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.0.tit: Filters are chosen when you run it, not when you build it
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.0.des: One report serves every month and every branch. Defining one per period is how you end up with forty reports that are the same report.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.1.tit: Changing the source clears the columns
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.1.des: The new source has different fields, so the old ones cannot be kept. Worth knowing before you touch it on a finished report.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.2.tit: Before you schedule it, see what it returns
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.2.des: A heavy report landing in twenty inboxes every morning is a burden nobody asked for. Run it first, schedule it after.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.3.tit: Totals are what make it a report
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.3.des: Which column adds up, which averages, and where the subtotal breaks. Without that it is a long list, not a report.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.4.tit: The report belongs to the company, not its author
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.4.des: What one person builds stays for everyone else. The question gets answered once, instead of each person answering it their own way.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.5.tit: The sources are limited on purpose
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.detalles.5.des: Exposing the whole database would allow queries that cross what must not be crossed. It is a security decision, not a limitation waiting to be lifted.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.pasos.0.descri: It determines which fields are available and what you can filter by.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.pasos.1.descri: Columns, filters, sorting and totals, seeing the result as you go.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.pasos.2.descri: With the filters you choose now, or let it arrive by email on its own.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.publico.0.titu: You are always missing a report
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.publico.0.desc: And waiting for someone to build it is not an option.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.publico.1.titu: You export to Excel every month
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.publico.1.desc: To rebuild the same cross-reference by hand, again.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.publico.2.desc: And remembering to is part of somebody's job.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.faq.0.pregunta: Do I need to know SQL?
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.faq.0.respuest: No. You pick the source and from there the columns, the filters, the sorting and the totals.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.faq.1.pregunta: Can I pull any data I want?
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.faq.1.respuest: Those in the curated sources, always scoped to your company. It is a security decision: there is no way to request another subscriber's data.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.faq.2.pregunta: Does it handle reports with line detail?
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.faq.2.respuest: Yes: header plus lines, which is the shape of most real business questions.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.faq.3.pregunta: What formats does it export to?
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.faq.3.respuest: PDF, Excel, CSV and TXT, and you can print straight from the screen.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.faq.4.respuest: Yes, at whatever interval you set. Worth running it first to see what it returns and who it makes sense to send it to.
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.faq.5.pregunta: Can I reproduce an old figure?
en.fun.generador-de-reportes.faq.5.respuest: Yes, through the run history: who ran it, when and with exactly which filters.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.subtitulo: Every screen explains what it does
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.resumen: 1,145 screens with their own help panel and 1,416 fields with their explanation, right inside the screen. No manuals, no training courses and no calls to support.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.heroTitulo: The help is where the doubt appears
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.heroBajada: 1,145 screens with their own help panel and 1,416 fields with an explanation right beside them. It is not a manual nobody opens: it is the text that appears exactly where the doubt appears.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.problema.titulo: An ERP nobody knows how to use is an ERP that goes unused
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.problema.texto: The real cost of a business system is not the licence: it is the time people take to learn how to use it. When the help is a three-hundred-page PDF, nobody opens it; they ask a colleague, fill the field by eye and the data goes in wrong. And that bad data later shows up in a report someone uses to make a decision.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.problema.puntos.0: The manual is a PDF nobody opens
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.problema.puntos.1: Every doubt is a call to support or to a colleague
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.problema.puntos.2: A field gets filled by eye and the data goes in wrong
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.problema.puntos.3: Training a new hire takes weeks
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.problema.puntos.4: The person who knows how to use it leaves and takes the knowledge with them
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.problema.puntos.5: There are screens the customer paid for and never uses
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.beneficios.0.descri: 1,145 screens explain what they solve and in what order they are used, from inside the screen itself. There is nothing to go looking for.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.beneficios.1.descri: 1,416 fields with what goes there and a real example. That is what prevents the guessed-at value, which is the one that later throws a report off.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.beneficios.2.titulo: Written in the terms of your business
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.beneficios.2.descri: The help says what it costs you in money, in time or in access — never how the software works inside. That is what makes it useful.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.beneficios.3.titulo: It warns about what throws no error
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.beneficios.3.descri: The traps that show no symptom are flagged: what changes more than it looks, what cannot be undone, what is calculated differently from what you assume.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.beneficios.4.descri: The tax, the receipt, the authority and the date format in the example are the ones where you operate, not those of another market.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.beneficios.5.titulo: It ships with the screen, not later
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.beneficios.5.descri: A new screen without its help turns the test suite red the same day. Nothing ships half-done.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.cifras.0.etiqueta: screens with their own help panel
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.detalles.0.titulo: Writing the help and wiring it up are two separate acts
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.detalles.0.descripc: And the second one shows no symptom: unwired, the panel simply does not render and nothing reports an error. That is why a test checks it, instead of trusting that someone will look.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.detalles.1.titulo: The example matters more than the definition
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.detalles.1.descripc: "October maintenance, contract 42" teaches more than "description of the debt". That is why every field carries a written example, not a repeated label.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.detalles.2.titulo: The warnings flag what cannot be undone
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.detalles.2.descripc: What cannot be undone, what changes more than it looks, and which decision drags the next ones with it. That is what a generic manual never tells you.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.detalles.3.titulo: It talks about your operation, not the code
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.detalles.3.descripc: Help that describes the interface does not help: the user is already looking at it. The useful kind says what a mistake there will cost them.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.detalles.4.descripc: ITBIS or VAT, DGII or SENIAT, NCF or e-invoice: the text is written once and reads correctly in each country.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.detalles.5.titulo: It cuts support, and support is money
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.detalles.5.descripc: Every doubt settled on the screen is a call that never happens. Across more than a thousand screens, that is the difference between using the system and fighting it.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.pasos.0.descripcion: The help panel is there, in the same place, every time.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.pasos.1.descripcion: Its explanation and example appear right beside it, without leaving the screen.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.pasos.2.descripcion: No manual, no course and no calling anyone.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.publico.0.descripci: And training each new person takes weeks.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.publico.1.titulo: You pay support for how-to questions
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.publico.1.descripci: That a good explanation would settle on its own.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.publico.2.descripci: Because nobody ever worked out what they were for.
en.fun.sistema-de-ayuda.faq.0.pregunta: Do I have to buy it separately?
